course.title: Gallbladder and bile duct disorders
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Intrahepatic biliary ducts - right and left intrahepatic bile ducts, right and left hepatic duct, join together to form common hepatic duct
  • Extrahepatic biliary tree – common hepatic duct and cystic duct form together common bile duct (CBD)
  • Cystic duct travels along CBD for about 1 cm, junction located right above duodenum, lots of anatomic variations
  • CBD = choledocus duct
    • Travels down along portal vein and proper hepatic artery, contact to medial wall of D2 duodenum and crossing posterior wall of D1 and posterior head of pancreas
    • Finally, entering into pancreas parenchyma and joining Wirsung duct = hepato-pancreatic duct
    • Opening at ampulla of Vater (D2 duodenum) with Oddi sphincter
    • CBD has 3 sections: supraduodenal, retroduodenal and intrapancreatic
  • Arterial blood supply of hepatocholedochal duct: right hepatic artery, proper hepatic artery, cystic artery, gastroduodenal artery and posterior pancreaticoduodenal artery
  • Venous drainage: paracholedochal venous plexus opening into portal vein
  • Innervation: parasympathetic vagal fibers and sympathetic fibers from celiac plexus
  • Normal sizes of CBD: 7-10 mm in diameter
  • Normal sizes of common hepatic duct: 5 mm
  • Normal sizes of cystic and intrahepatic ducts: 1-3 mm in diameter
  • Gallbladder/ cholecyst = diverticulum of CBD, 7-10 cm, situated inferior of segment V
    • Its fundus reaching anterior liver margin, body and infundibulum heading posterior towards CBD
    • Anteriorly – anterior abdominal wall and inferior aspect of liver
    • Posteriorly – transverse colon and first two portions of duodenum
    • Arterial blood supply of gallbladder: cystic artery dividing into anterior and posterior branches at level of gallbladder neck
    • Gallbladder veins draining directly into intrahepatic portal branches, rarely into cystic vein
    • Lymphatic drainage: directly into liver or into celiac lymph nodes through Mascagni’s lymph node
    • Innervation: sympathetic fibers originating from celiac plexus, parasympathetic fibers of vagal origin
  • Cholecystectomy safety triangle = Calot triangle → cystic duct, right side of CBD and inferior face of liver;

crossed by cystic artery

Physiology

  • Bile = main exocrine liver secretion → 1000-1500 ml day
  • Produced by hepatocytes
  • Normal bile pressure = 9-10 cm H2O in CBD, 8-10 cm H2O in gallbladder
  • Pressure increases to 14-18 cm H2O during cholecystitis or 25 cm H2O in colic
  • Bile is predispose to stasis (especially in disturbance of vagus nerve → e.g., gastrectomy)
  • Composition: water mixed with cholesterol, phospholipids (lecithin), bile salts (mainly chenodeoxicholic and cholic acid) and conjugated bilirubin (breakdown product of haemoglobin)
  • Cholesterol is not water soluble → mixing with phospholipids and bile salts → micelles
  • When proportion of bile constituents is unbalanced → bile becomes lithogenic
  • Between meals, sphincter of Oddi is closed top revent reflux and bile accumulating into gallbladder
  • During meals, under neuro hormonal influences, gallbladder pushes its content
  • Bile is acting as detergent, emulsifying fats to facilitate digestion
  • Bile salts/ pigments resorbed in distal ileum and portal venous system back to liver = enterohepatic circulation
  • Absence of distal small bowel → reducing quantity of bile salts in bile → bile becomes lithogenic
  • Absence of bile in intestine (external bile drainage, obstructive jaundice) → malabsorption of fats, fat soluble vitamins (A,D,E,K), alteration of intestinal microbial flora and impairment of intestinal wall trophicity
  • Morphine causes contraction of Oddi sphincter → counter indicated in colics and acute pancreatitis !!!
  • Relaxation of sphincter → spasmolitics, nitrates, miophilin, curara, lydocain

Imaging

Non-invasiveInvasive

- Essential

diameter of ducts
- Not choice for detecting CBD lithiasis (duodenal gas)		1. Endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography
(ERCP)

instrumentation of CBD
- Remove stones or insert stents
- Severe complication (acute pancreatitis, perforation of
ducts/ duodenum, peritonitis, bleeding, allergy to
contrast, acute cholangitis, acute cholecystitis) !!!
- Not used for diagnostic purposes !!!
Indication
- confirmed CBD stones
- high risk/probability of CBD stones, persistent jaundice
- CBD > 8/10 mm diameter
- acute cholangitis
Contraindication
- Main organ failures with high risk of sedation
- Severe coagulation disorders
- Tight esophageal, gastric or duodenal stenoses (no
passage of endoscope)
2. Abdominal plain X-ray

with normal US

    • intraoperative ultrasound
    • intraoperative cholangioscopy

Lab test

  • Without complications → normal lab tests
  • Leukocytosis: acute cholecystitis, empyema of cholecyst or severe cholangitis
  • Prothrombintime: checked especially in prolonged jaundice, lack of bile impairs absoption of vitamin K
  • Bilirubin (total and conjugated): raised in obstructive jaundice → severe acute cholecystitis, obstacle in CBD; should drop after surgery, otherwise suggests incomplete procedure
  • Alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamil transpeptidase: cholestasis
  • 5-nucleotidase: more sensitive marker of cholestasis
  • Transaminases (ASAT, ALAT): hepatocytolisis in severe cholecystitis and cholangitis

Gallbladder lithiasis

Causes

  • 1. Lithogenic bile secretion (inborn, diet)
  • 2. Biliary stasis (anatomical, functional)
  • 3. Infection in biliary tree
  • 4. Abnormalities of gallbladder epithelium
LithogenicAnti-lithogenic
Rise of cholesterol or loss of bile salt
- High protein, fat diet, low residue diet
- Contraceptive pill, pregnancy
- Obesity
- Loss of terminal ileum (enterohepatic circulation)
- Gastric resection, truncal vagotomy
- Total parenteral nutrition
- Chronic octreotide treatment
- Hemolitic anemia		- Bile salts
→ Lecithin
→ Apolipoprotein A, B
→ Ursodeoxicolic acid

3 types of stones

  • Cholesterol stones: solitary or multiple, different sizes, high levels of blood cholesterol are risk factor, pregnancy, contraceptive pill, family history, obesity, low dietary fibre
  • Pigment stones: irregular, black and small in size, looking as covered with thorns, composed of calcium bilirubinate and carbonate, in haemolytic anaemia
  • Mixed stones: most common, varying size, shape and colour, formed by mix of cholesterol and bile pigments

Clinical aspects

  • Asymptomatic 80%
  • Biliar dispepsia snd = non-specific symptoms: migraine, headache, nausea, vomiting, dull pain in epigastrum or

right abdominal quadrant

  • Pain → 2-3 hours after meal in right hypocondrum or epigastrum, severe in intensity, increases progressively,

lasting for several hours, radiation to inferior scapula

  • Nausea, vomiting, sweating
  • Hypostenic syndrome → bloating, eructation, fatty-food intolerance, post-prandial somnolence, morning bitter taste
  • Hyperstenic syndrome → post-prandial diarrhea, migraines, iritability
  • Biliary colic (cholecyst contracting against obstacle, outflow of bile blocked → dilating gallbladder)
  • Fever (acute cholecytsitis)
  • Acute pancreatis

Complications

Occure when stones gets stuck (usually narrow parts - infundibulum, cystic duct, sphincter of Oddi)

  • a) Infectious – acute cholecystitis
  • b) Chronic cholecystitis
  • c) Mechanical obstruction by migration of stones
  • d) Mechano-inflammatory - fistulas
  • e) Degenerative – gallbladder carcinoma

DD

  • I. Acute cholecystitis
  • II. Acute appendicitis
  • III. Perforated duodenal ulcer
  • IV. Acute pancreatitis
  • V. Hepatic diseases (hepatitis, abscesses)
  • VI. Renal colic
  • VII. Myocardial infarction
  • VIII. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome
a) Acute cholecystitis
obstruction
  • Obstruction → concentrated bile → irritated mucosa → inflammatory process → infection
  • Catarrhal → phlegmonous → gangrenous
  • Thickening of wall (edema, inflammation)
  • Bile becomes purulent ±

Clinical

  • Pain – usually of sudden onset, may first be colicky, then constant and throbbing, right hypochondrium
  • Nausea and vomiting – common, mild in nature
  • Pyrexia/ fever and tachycardia
  • Signs: tenderness → guarding and rigidity
  • Palpable painful mass (distended cholecyst and inflammatory adhesions to great omentum, duodenum, colon

= subhepatic block)

  • Murphy’s sign +

Diagnosis/ work-up

  • Lab tests: WBC ↑, ASAT, ALAT ↑ (±), BB, AF, GGT, AMY ↑ (±)
  • US → distended gallbladder, thickening of the wall (double layer wall)

Evolution

  • Resolution (stone falls back into gallbladder, but recurrence is almost rule)
  • Progression to gangrene and perforation
  • Gallbladder accumulates mucus → distended, tension, clear transparent content – hydrocholecyst/ hydrops
  • Large stones, rarely swollen gallbladder can press against CBD -> producing obstructive jaundice = Mirrizzi snd
  • Empyema of gallbladder
  • Subhepatic block and subhepatic abscess

Treatment

  • 1. Intravenous fluids and nil by mouth
  • 2. Pain relief (iv and ice-bag on right hypochondrum)
  • 3. Antibiotics
  • 4. Surgical intervention – cholecystectomy/stomy
  • Cholecystectomy for acute Cholecystitis
  • Moment → early/ late
  • Early cholecystectomy
Pro’s- Easier to dissect, no sclerosis
- Short hospitalization
- Early recover
Contra’s- Modified anatomy due to inflammation
- Difficulties in elements recognition
- Prone to iatrogenic injuries
  • b) Chronic cholecystitis
    • After repeated episodes of inflammatory attacks → gallbladder’s wall become rigid, fibrotic, moulded on calculi (scleroatrophic cholecystitis) or thick, hypertrophied wall (sclerohypertrophic cholecystitis)
    • Bile content with/ without infected
    • Recurrent bouts of abdominal pain, without fever
    • Fatty meals cause abdominal discomfort and flatulence
    • Attacks of acute cholecystitis can occur
    • DD: chronic dyspepsia (e.g., peptic ulcer), hiatus hernia, coronary insufficiency
  • c) Mechanical obstruction
    • Stones often causes obstruction of CBD
  • d) Mechano-inflammatory complications => fistula
  • Bilio-biliar fistula → Mirizzi snd; always cause choledocholithiasis
  • Bilio-digestive fistula → gallbladder ileus
  • e) Degenerative complications
  • Gallbladder CA
  • In 65-90% bile stones are associated
  • Over 60 years of age
  • When associated with stones, more frequent in women
  • Big stones→ chronic inflammation → dysplasia → Neoplasia

Imaging

  • Abdominal US and MRI/ MRCP for diagnosis
  • ERCP for treatment only: removal of stones

Treatment

Medication

  • High rates of failure, recurrence is a rule
  • Bile acid based (ursodeoxycholic acid) → changing chemical composition of bile
  • Life time intake
  • Takes months or years to dissolve a stone
  • Decreasing size makes them susceptible to migrate
  • Reserved for those reject surgery or who are not suitable

Surgery

Cholecystectomy- Whenever it is possible
- Open by laparotomy or laparoscopic
- Dissection, ligation and section of cystic duct and cystic artery in Calot triangle and dissection
of gallbladder from liver fossa
- Retrograde cholecystectomy: dissection progress from cystic towards fundus
- Anterograde cholecystectomy: towards pedicle of gallbladder
Cholecystostomy- Connection between gallbladder and exterior, extracting stones and draining bile liquid
- Patients unsuitable for OR, with acute cholecystitis or obstructive CBD stones

Special situations

  • Symptomless gallstone
    • No consensus if surgery is indicated or not
    • Most patient will remain asymptomatic
    • Prophylactic cholecystectomy is not generally recommended for prevention of gallbladder cancer
    • Advised to prevent complications: young patient with large stones, haemolytic stones, transplant recipie.
  • Acute cholecystitis
    • Surgery is best option
    • Intervention done in first 24-72 hours after onset
    • Prior → iv hydration, broad spectrum antibiotics, antispastics, antialgics
    • Extraction of infected cholecyst in a plastic bag to protect abdominal wall from suppuration
    • Even in subhepatic block → gentle and careful blunt dissection
    • After operation, antibiotherapy no longer required
  • Biliary fistulas
    • Require cholecystectomy and repairing of digestive tract
    • Usually by open approach
  • Intrabiliary fistulas
    • Challenging (hard to repair, Calot triangle severely modified, raising risk of vascular lesions)
    • Exact diagnosis and complete mapping of biliary tract before intervention mandatory
    • Cholecystectomy and biliary repair by Roux en Y hepatico jejunostomy

Common bile duct lithiasis

  • Occurs in 11-20% of cases
  • 2nd most common complication
  • Gallbladder stone can migrate into common bile duct (most common)
  • In few situations, originates from choledocus duct itself (primary duct stones) or from intrahepatic ducts (i.e. Caroli

disease, inflammatory bile duct stenosis)

  • Stenosis/ obstruction → duct dilatation and infection

Risk factors

  • Migrated stones
    • Small size of stones (3-5 mm)
    • Large cystic duct
    • Gallbladder with contractile walls
    • Residual cystic duct stones after cholecystectomy, particular appearance of cystic duct = “double barrel shotgun sign”, can cause recurrent choledocholithiasis
    • Long evolution of cholecystolithiasis, hight risk of concomitant CBD stones
  • Primary stones
    • Sclerosing cholangitis
    • Parasitic infection (Clonorchis sinensis)
    • Stenosis of the biliary tree (chronic cephalic pancreatitis, (iatrogenic) post traumatic)
    • Caroli disease
    • Benign stenosis of the sphincter of Oddi (sclerosing odditis)
    • Mirizzi syndrome type I
  • a) Primary common bile duct stones
    • Rare (4%)
    • Only when bile stasis in CBD
    • Stenosis → inflammation → infection → germs release beta glucuronidase → deconjugate conjugated bilirubin → unconjugated bilirubin precipitates → pigment calculi
  • b) Migrated common bile duct stones
    • Most frequent
    • CBD stones have same gross appearance and composition as gallbladder stones (blackberry like, hard, predominantly of cholesterin)
    • Migration either by “ natural route” or through fistula between gallbladder and main bile duct
    • Mirizzi syndrome
Type 1extrinsic compression of common hepatic duct (CHD)
Type 2erosion of CHD wall and formation of cholecystocholedochal fistula (up to 1/3 CHD wall involved)
Type 3up to 2/3 of CHD wall circumference involved in cholecystocholedochal fistula
Type 4entire CHD wall involved in cholecystocholedochal fistula
Type 5any of above with cholecysto-enteric fistula

Pathophysilogy

  • Bergman’s triad: calculus migrated in common bile duct → bile stasis (cholestasis) → superinfection (cholangitis)
  • Depending on size of stone
    • can pass through sphincter of Oddi into duodenum (80%)
    • get stuck at Vater’s ampula → upwards distension and biliary obstruction → angiocholitis
  • Spasm and hyperpressure translate into pain (choledochal colic) and biliary stasis → infection (chills, fever)
  • Might be resolved by passage of stone through sphincter (increased pressure) or stone disimpacts and falls back into dilated CBD (recurrency at any time) = “floating” stones
  • In partial obstruction of CBD → still increase in bile pressure → repeated episodes of cholangitis
    • liver fibrosis and inflammation = secondary biliary cirrhosis
  • “rock paving” = paradoxical variant that consists of accumulation of many calculi in CBD without manifest jaundice, bile flowing like “ river water through rocks”
  • “icterus melas” = clinical features resemble malignant biliary obstruction
  • “satellite hepatitis” = CBD obstruction over extended time → hepatocytolysis
  • Acute biliary pancreatitis particularly caused by migration of small calculi (< 5 mm), regurgitation of bile into Wirsung duct and local activation of pancreatic enzymes !

Clinical features

  • PAIN -> FEVER -> JAUNDICE – Charcot-Villard triad (most distinct manifestation; in this order otherwise, other

diagnosis are more likely)

  • Pain – distension, right upper quadrant and epigastric (Chauffard’s choledochopancreatic zone), intense, steady,

backwards irradiated, 4-6 hours after ingestion of cholecystokinetic meal

  • Fever – angyocholitis, begins with intense chills, 3-4 h after
  • Jaundice – obstruction, at 12-24h or later, usually varying in intensity, yellow red/greenish, might cause dark urine

and pale stool

  • Only present in 45-50% of cases
  • Onset usually sudden
  • Long standing cases might show pruritus
  • Other findings: xanthelasma; scratching lesions; painful sensitivity; hepatomegaly, late altered of general condition

Atypical forms

  • Minor choledochal syndrome/ forme fruste: minor pain, chills, dark urine
  • Feverish/ angiocholitic form: bilio-septic fever of Chauffard, irregular, short febrile episodes, profuse sweating

episodes, pseudo malaria

  • Hyperacute form: most dangerous form, a potentially lethal, rapidly evolves towards severe acute cholangitis,

acute concomitant liver and kidney failure, septic-toxic shock, surgical emergency

  • Dyspeptic form – confusion with other gastrointestinal disorders
  • Cachectic form – weight loss
  • Mute form – very rare
  • Pseudoneoplastic form – jaundice, no pain
  • Ictero-uremigen angyocholitis Caroli
  • Biliary secondary cirrhosis

DD

  • DD of obstructive jaundice
    • Hepatic jaundice (acute hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug related cholestasis, liver poisoning, liver tumors)
    • Posthepatic jaundice caused by other conditions than stones (congenital and postraumatic strictures, sclerosing cholangitis, bile duct tumors, external compression made by periampulary tumors, pancreatitis, hilar lymphadenopathy)
  • DD for pain
    • Peptic ulcer
    • Renal colic
    • Iobstruction
    • Angina pectoris
    • Acute pancreatitis (can mimic cbd stones, but it can also be caused by them)

Lab exam

  • Renal function should be carefully monitored in patients with choledocholithiasis → serious risk for toxaemic

concomitant renal failure !

  • Serum and urine amylases for monitoring pancreatic reaction

Imaging

  • US (CBD > 8mm, multiple small stones in gallbladder), PTC, ERCP, MRCP

Criteria for prediction of common bile duct stones

  • Very high probability Clinically: acute cholangitis Laboratory: total bilirubin exceeding 4 mg/dl Imaging: confirmation of CBD stones by ultrasound
  • High probability >50% Laboratory: total bilirubin over 1.7 mg/dl Imaging: EHBD dilation on ultrasound
  • Moderate probability of CBDS < 10-50% Clinically: biliary pancreatitis, age over 55 years Laboratory: altered hepatic tests (other than bilirubin)
  • Low probability of CBDS < 10% Clinically: absence of jaundice Imaging: absence of EHBD dilations

Treatment

  • Fluid and electrolyte replacement, antibiotics, antispasmodic, painkillers (No Morphine!!)
  • Protection of liver cell
  • If jaundice is prolonged – vit. K, plasma
  • Immediate bile drainage is mandatory in angiocholitis

Complications Early

  • Acute pancreatitis (most common)
  • Hemorrhage from sphincterotomy (only if Hb falls by 2g or melena) (frequent in

cirrhosis, coagulation disorders, chronic anticoagulant, chronic renal failure,re- sphincterotomy, incorrect orientation of endoscope)

  • Duodenal perforation: fistula – peritonitis/retro-peritonitis
  • CBD perforation: biliary fistulae – choleperitoneum
  • Angiocholitis/ cholangitis
  • Impaction of extraction basket

Late

  • Papillary stenosis:

Other non-surgical techniques for CBD stones

  • Percutaneous extraction
  • Combined technique → Radiological-endoscopical – intrahepatic and CBD stones (through cholecystostomy)
  • b) Laparoscopic surgery
    • Concomitant laparoscopic treatment of cholecystolithiasis and choledocholithiasis is Gold standart

Transcystic CBD approach

  • Fist surgical choice
  • Indications
    • Failure of endoscopic CBD stone extraction
    • Contraindications of choledochotomy
      • ➔CBD diameter < 6mm
      • ➔Sclerosing pediculitis
      • ➔Impossibility to suture choledochotomy site
    • Stones less than 6-8 mm
  • Contraindications
    • Stones > 6 mm
    • Intrahepatic lithiasis
    • A cystic duct caliber < 4 mm
    • A cystic duct with posterior insertion
    • A cystic duct with distal insertion (double barrel shotgun)
  • Technique
    • Exploratory stage (cholangiography)
    • Transcystic access to CBD
    • Administration of 1 mg glucagon i.v. with relaxation of oddian sphincter
    • Inserted catheter removal of small stones (< 4 mm) by lavage with saline (low pressure)
    • Control cholangiography or/and choledochoscopy
    • In failure or larger stones, extraction with dormia or foley catheters
    • Clipping and sectioning of cystic duct and cholecystectomy
    • Leaving transcystic duct drainage catheter in place for 15-18 days

Choledochotomy

  • Indications
    • A large number of stones
    • Stones situated proximally to the cystic duct insertion
    • Stones larger than 8 mm
    • Impossibility of transcystic access
    • Failure of transcystic approach
    • Contraindications of transcystic approach
  • Contraindications
    • CBD caliber < 5 6 mm
    • Pediculitis/peripediculitis that makes impossible the dissection and identification of CBD
    • Impossibility of CBD suture
    • Portal hypertension (“pericholedochal varices”)
  • Technique
    • CBD visualized
    • 2 guiding threads placed – traction on anterior side of supraduodenal common bile duct
    • Longitudinal supraduodenal choledochotomy along long axis of duct
    • Cbd lavage under pressure to drive small stones through papilla or choledochotomy site (risk for mobilized upstream (intrahepatically))
    • Instrumental extraction of stones (basket or balloon catheters)
    • Large stones require intraductal lithotripsy
    • Finally, choledochoscopy and cholangiography
    • Closure by...
    • Primary coledochorrhaphy – primary suture, without biliary drainage, superior to others
    • External drainage of common bile duct with T tube
      • ➔Advantages: effective biliary decompression in case of papillary edema or residual stone fragments; allows postoperative radiological control (T tube cholangiography); easy access for extraction of potential residual stones without using postoperative endoscopic sphincterotomy
      • ➔14 Fr T tubes
      • ➔Sutured tightly around tube
      • ➔End of tube will be externalized through percutaneous orifice
      • ➔Control by T tube cholangiography
      • ➔Effective external drainage of the common bile duct
      • ➔Removed 10-14 days postoperatively, after final control cholangiography

Indications

  • Failure or contraindications of preoperative ERCP
  • Failure or contraindications of laparoscopic approach
  • Impossible access to endoscopy or/and laparoscopy
  • Detection of CBDS during open cholecystectomy
  • Large stones
  • Impacted stones in the papilla
  • Indications for biliodigestive derivation
    • CBD rock paving
    • marked CBD dilations (≥ 20 mm)
    • benign CBD stenosis (chronic pancreatitis)
    • primary (autochthonous) CBD stones
  • Gastric resection with Billroth II reconstruction or total gastrectomy with Roux en Y reconstruction
  • Gastroenteroanastomosis
  • Juxtapapillary duodenal diverticulum

Contraindications

  • Portal hypertension from cirrhosis or portal vein thrombosis –major risk is exuberant collateral venous circulation in hepatic pedicle (“pericholedochal varices”)
  • CBD caliber < 5-6 mm – high risk of late stenosis at common bile duct suture site
  • Sclerosing pediculitis – sclero-inflammatory changes make dissection and identification of CBD impossible
  • Acute cholangitis with septic shock – emergency biliary decompression, initially minimally invasive (endoscopic) and subsequently surgical

Technique

  • CBD exploration, clearance (choledochotomy and intraoperative cholangiography, instrumental extraction), choledochotomy closure (primary suture or T tube)

Intrahepatic stones

  • Prevalent in East Asia, rare in western countries
  • Majority - brown pigment stones (soft and friable)
  • Etiology: bile stasis, bacterial infection, biliary mucin i.e. intrahepatic bile duct cyst, stenosis,

Clinical aspect: RQ pain (70%), jaundice + fever (30%), abdominal discomfort + vomiting, asymptomatic (16%)

Effects: chronic proliferative /suppurative/granulomatous cholangitis

Diagnostics

  • US, CT, MRCP, ERCP
  • Best solution → PTC followed by drainage and ductoscopy

Treatment

  • Drainage of affected bile ducts
  • Removal of stones, treatment of causes (i.e. stenosis)
  • Percutaneous cholangioscopy (with electrohydraulic/laser lithotripsy)
  • Hepatic resection can removes stones and causes

Bile duct cysts

  • Congenital lesions

Clinical aspect

  • Jaundice
  • Pain
  • Tumoral mass

Complications

  • Angiocholitis
  • CBD stones
  • Biliary cirrhosis
  • - Cholangiocarcinoma

APBDU

Long common channel, perpendicular confluent angle

Treatment

  • Resection and hepatico-jejunanastomosis

Caroli disease → multiple intrahepatic cysts that communicates with bile ducts

  • Local or diffuse
  • ± congenital liver fibrosis
  • Angiocholitis, stone formation → cirrhosis
  • Treatment: Hepatic resection in localized form Liver transplant

Sclerosing cholangitis (SC)

= Fibrosing and inflammatory obstruction of bile ducts

  • Underlying etiology → secondary sclerosing cholangitis (SSC)
  • Idiopathic → primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
  • Clinical: recurrent fever, RUQ pain, jaundice, pruritus
  • a) SSC
  • Lesions are isolated or diffuse
  • Could affect intra- or extrahepatic bile ducts

Etiology

  • Formaldehyde injection of hepatic hydatid cyst
  • Prior hepato-biliary surgery or trauma
  • Ischemic strictures
  • Choledocolithiasis
  • Intra-arterial injection of floxuridine
  • Bile duct carcinoma
  • AIDS + infection with Cryptosporidium, cytomegalovirus, microsporidium
  • Autoimmune hepatitis

Treatment

  • resection and bilio-enteric anastomosis
  • Endoscopic balloon dilatation/ stenting
  • b) PCS
  • Immune mediated disease

Diagnostic criteria

  • 1. Absence of previous operative trauma to biliary system
  • 2. Sclerosis and stenosis involving all/ most extrahepatic bile ducts
  • 3. Exclusion of biliary malignant disease ±
  • 4. Absence of lithiasis

Lab

  • AF ↑ 2-3 folds, ASAT/ ALAT ↑, BB fluctuant (if raises → stenosis, cancer, stones, angiocholitis)

Imaging

  • ERCP, MRCP, PTC – strictures at all levels
  • Strictures alternating with ectasia – aspect of pruning and beading of biliary tree

Associated diseases (PSC)

  • Chronic ulcerative colitis
  • Crohn’s colitis
  • Chronic pancreatitis
  • Celiac disease
  • Pulmonary infiltrates
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Glomerulonephritis

Evolution

  • Progress to liver failure – median survival 12 years after diagnostic

Complications

  • Severe pruritus
  • Steatorrhea
  • Deficiencies in vit ADEK
  • Portal hypertension, biliar cirrhosis
  • Specific complications: acalculous cholecystitis, biliar calculi with cholangitis, cholangiocarcinoma

Treatment

  • Non-surgical: almost ineffective (corticosteroids, UDCA)
  • Sphincterotomy seems to be beneficial
  • Stent insertion, balloon dilatation
  • Surgical: biliary reconstruction
  • Orthotopic liver transplantation

Alithiasic gallbladder diseases

Acalculous acute
cholecystitis		- Often encountered in severe septic conditions – septicemias, salmonellosis, severe burns,
trauma, postoperative, post chemotherapy, AIDS
- Important ischemia in walls
- Evolution - fast and severe
- Clinical: as a calculous cholecystitis, more severe
- Treatment: cholecystostomy in very ill patients
CholecystosisAdenomiomatosis of the gallbladder
= Mucosal hyperplasia and glandular hyperplasia → glandes of Luschka, or
invaginations of the mucosa, reaching the serosa- sinus of Rokitansky-Aschof
→ localized in the infundibulum
Cholesterolosis
→ Cholesterol deposits on the gallbladder’s mucosa
- Big crystals of cholesterol loose from the mucosa – are acting as stones
- Clinical: as gallbladder lithiasis, but more prone to cause acute pancreatitis

Bilio-digestive fistula

  • Aberrant connections formed between element of extrahepatic bile ducts (gallbladder or common bile duct) and

digestive tract (stomach, duodenum, colon)

  • Rare (<5%)
  • Most common (80%): cholecysto-duodenal fistulas
  • Other types s. oben

Etiology

  • Lithiasic origin (90%)
  • Post traumatic (e.g., Crohn disease)
  • Iatrogenic – cholecystostomy
  • Oddi sphincterotomy
  • Alveolar echinococcosis
  • Chronic duodenal ulcer (2nd most common)
  • Neoplastic (invasion and erosison of wall)
    • Distal common bile duct cancer
    • Carcinoma of ampulla of Vater
    • Neoplasm of head of pancreas
    • Duodenal neoplasms
    • Gallbladder cancer
    • Colon cancer

Lithiasic fistula

Large stone → obstruction of cystic duct → recurrent episodes of acute or chronic cholecystitis

  • constant increasing pressure → ischemia of wall → focal necrosis
  • inflammatory adhesions to adjacent organs (adhesion block)
  • stone will penetrate gallbladder wall and its digestive partner

Clinical manifestation

  • Frequently asymptomatic (frequently detected only during surgery)
  • Common clinical manifestations
    • Abdominal pain (epigastric, right upper quadrant, intermittent cramps, Konig syndrome (migrated, obstructive large stones)
    • Nausea, vomiting
    • Weight loss
    • Diarrhea (typical in cholecysto colic fistulas)
  • Acute clinical manifestations
    • Cholangitis (pain, fever, jaundice) result of contaminating digestive reflux in cholecysto colic fistulas
    • Upper digestive hemorrhage (melena) – intermittent, small amounts, due to fistular erosion into visceral wall
    • Biliary ileus
      • ➔Rare variant of acute bowel obstruction, sudden onset, abundant vomiting, central abdominal distension, cessation of bowel movements, altered general state
      • ➔Migration of large gallbladder stone (3-4 cm) through large cholecysto-duodenal fistula, sudden obstructive at terminal ileum (60%), exceptionally at level of ileo cecal valve
      • ➔Predominantly in elderly female patients
      • ➔Long history of gallbladder calculi (20-40 years)
      • ➔Less common locations for obstruction – jejunum, left colon, upper rectum
    • Bouveret syndrome
      • ➔Rarely as result of biliary ileus
      • ➔= proximal obstructive impaction of very large stone at level of duodenal bulb or inferior duodenal flexure
      • ➔Clinical manifestations like in proximal acute bowel obstructions (frequent vomiting, water-electrolyte imbalance, rapid alteration of general state)

Imaging

  • Plain abdominal X ray
    • RIGLER’s triad: Air fluid levels (small bowel type), Aerobilia, large radiopaque mass with atypical location
    • BALTHAZAR – SCHECHTER sign: presence of air in gallbladder
  • Percutaneous abdominal ultrasound: aerobilia, scleroatrophic gallbladder, residual gallstones
  • Contrast enhanced CT
  • ERCP
  • MRCP – high accuracy
  • Gastroduodenoscopy: reveals cause of obstruction in Bouveret syndrome with direct vision

Treatment

  • Cholecysto-duodenal or cholecysto-colic fistulas
    • Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
    • Laparoscopic suture of fistular orifice (duodenal or colonic)
  • Neoplastic cholecysto-colic fistulas
    • Primary tumor is colic (right flexure or right transverse) - right hemicolectomy with cholecystectomy
    • Gallbladder cancer - surgical resection rarely possible
  • Choledocho-duodenal fistulas generated by duodenal ulcers (80%)
    • Angiocholitis without CBD stenosis - treating ulcer with medication
    • Biliary stenoses +/- cholangitis - 2/3 gastric resection, gastro-jejunostomy, vagotomy and bilio digestive diversions
  • Choledochoduodenal fistulas of malignant etiology
    • Endoscopic stent placement (non resectable cases) or by pancreatico-duodenectomy (periampullary tumors)

Gallbladder CA

= most frequent malignancy of biliary tract

  • very aggressive
  • 5-year survival is around 5-10%
  • Only 1 in 5 patients is diagnosed at early stage

Risk factors

  • Chronic inflammation 95% – gallstones (particularly large), cholecysto-enteric fistulas, porcelain gallbladder

(calcification of wall)

  • Adenomas/ polyps of gallbladder – papillary, villous, > 10 mm
  • Carcinogenic substances: nitrosamines, rubber industry
  • Anomalous junction between Wirsung and choledoc with long common channel – chronic angiocholitis
  • Choledochal cysts
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Obesity
  • Female sex

Pathogenesis

  • Hyperplasia → metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma
  • Hyperplasia = reaction to chronic inflammation
  • Metaplasia = chronic irritation – pseudopiloric metaplasia (66-84%), gastric metaplasia (25-50%), intestinal

metaplasia (12-52%)

  • Dysplasia = in situ carcinoma

Histology

  • Adenocarcinomas (90 %)
  • Squamous cell carcinomas (10 %)
  • Undifferentiated carcinomas
  • Infiltrates gallbladder wall quickly, then adjacent organs especially liver

Clinical

  • Symptoms are stones related or mimicking biliary colic/ chronic cholecystitis
  • Changing of pain features – RUQ, deep, intense, stubborn 75%
  • Weight loss, asthenia, fatigue 60%
  • Jaundice 50%
  • Mass in right hypochondrium 50%
  • Hepatomegaly 40%
  • Fever 25%

Pattern of spread

  • Lymphatic
  • Hematogenous
  • Direct extension
  • Perineural
  • Intraductal

Diagnostics

  • Lab test: cholestasis enzymes ↑, conjugated BB ± ↑, Prothrombin time prolonged,
  • Tumoral markers: CA 19-9 > 20 units/ml , CEA > 4 ng/ml
  • Gene mutation: p53, K-ras
  • Imaging tests: US (abdominal, endoscopic) first intent, CT, MRI/ MRCP, PET, Cholangiography

Staging → TNM

Though serosa

Treatment

Stage ITumor invading muscularis propria →Cholecystectomy+/- lymphadenectomy
Stage IIInvasion of subserosa → radicalCholecystectomy+ regional lymphadenectomy
Stage III, IVaInvasion of liver parenchyma or other organs →extended cholecystectomy, en bloc resection
Stage IVbPalliative → biliary drainage → endoscopy, surgery

Surgery

  • Cholecystectomy with liver resection limited to segments IV and V + periportal lymphadenectomy
  • Extended liver and bile duct resection may be necessary in advanced disease for Ro margins + other organs (duodenum, pancreas)
  • Open approach is preferred (laparotomy)

Chemotherapy & Radiotherapy

  • Pre- and postoperatively chemo
  • Pre-OP stops development and decreases tumor size
  • Post-OP minimize risk of relapse
  • Postoperative radiotherapy in tumors > T2

Unresectable tumors

  • Distant metastasis or invasion in celiac or aorto-caval lymph nodes
  • Palliative approach → biliary drainage + chemo

Cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct neoplasm)

  • Rare tumor (0,1-2%)
  • 2nd most common liver tumor after HCC
  • 40-65 years
  • Mortality rate is high

Risk factors

  • Chronic inflammaion
  • 1. Bile stasis and ductal stones
  • 2. PSC
  • 3. Parasites - clonorchis sinensis
  • 4. Bile duct cysts and anomalous pancreato-choledocal junction
  • 5. Certain chemicals
  • 6. Cirrhosis
  • 7. IBD
  • 8. Old age
  • 9. Obesity
  • 10. Alcohol consumption and smoking

Morphopatholgy

  • Adenocarcinoma
  • Less frequent: sarcomas, lymphomas, small cell neoplasms, adenosquamous and squamous carcinoma
  • Benign lesions: hamartomas and adenomas
  • Sclerosing, Nodular or Papillary
  • Nodular growth with periductal infiltration, in time leads to lumen stenosis

Classification

  • Intrahepatic - Superior 1/3
    • from branches of intrahepatic biliary tree
    • similar to neoplasm originating in hepatocyte (HCC) → treated similarly
    • 10% of all cholangiocarcinomas
  • Perihilar - Middle 1/3 → Klatskin tumor
    • extrahepatic
    • from bile ducts located in hepatic hilum
    • 60-70% of all bile duct tumours
  • Distal - Inferior 1/3 → Periampullary tumor
    • extrahepatic
    • last portion of main bile duct
  • similar to pancreatic head tumors → similar treatment
  • 20-30% of all cholangiocarcinomas

= Klatskin-Bismuth classification

Clinical

  • Mainly asymptomatic, symptoms only when size increases or obstruction of bile duct lumen
  • Pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, pale stool (advanced stage)
  • Pain – RUQ
  • Weight loss, asthenia, fatigue
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Fever, chills
  • Variation according to location
    • Intrahepatic - nonspecific symptoms, upper abdominal pain, asthenia, fatigue, cachexia
    • Perihilar - biliary obstruction with painless jaundice (approximately 90%) and cholestasis, 10% have cholangitis, 50% systemic symptoms (abdominal discomfort, malaise, nausea, weight loss)
    • Distal - similar to perihilar, mimic symptoms of pancreatic head neoplasms, obstruction of common hepatobiliary duct can cause acute pancreatitis

DD jaundice → benign and malignant obstructive j.

  • Benign: sudden onset, fever and biliary colic, positive Murphy sign, positive inflammatory markers, imaging shows gallbladder or bile duct lithiasis
  • Malignant: insidious onset, without pain or fever, slow progression, positive Curvoisier-Terrier sign, positive tumor markers, tumoral masses, lymphadenopathy, ascites

Diagnostics

  • Lab: cholestasis enzymes ↑, conjugated BB ± ↑, Prothrombin time prolonged
  • Tumor markers: CA 19.9, CA 125, CEA and AFP
  • Gene mutation in p53

Imaging

  • US → first intent, detection, extrahepatic lesions hard to see
  • MRCP, gadolinium enhanced MRI → method of choice for diagnosis
  • CT → staging
  • EUS → FNAB, strictures or periampullary tumors
  • Cholangiography (ERCP, PTC) → to distinguish benign from malignant biliary strictures and for FNAB or biliary drainage
  • FDG PET → good for metastasis, limited use for primary tumor (hilar and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas are infiltrative → not readily detected by PET, limited effect due to infectious and inflammatory lesions)

Staging → TNM

  • Intrahepatic tumors are staged differently from extrahepatic ones

Treatment

a. Surgery b. Chemotherapy c. Radiotherapy d. Palliation

a. Surgery

  • Either curative or palliative
  • Only small proportion of biliary neoplasms are resectable at diagnosis
  • Surgical treatment vary accordingly to localizations of cholangiocarcinomas
  • High complication risk: postoperative bleeding, anastomotic fistulas and liver injury, anastomotic stenoses
    • Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
    • Surgical resection = only curative treatment
    • Most patients are inoperable → tumor too advanced
    • Surgery contraindicated in case of multiple tumors, periportal adenopathy and distant metastases
    • R0 margin not clearly established
    • R0 resection in patients without distant metastases → higher survival
    • R0 margin in patients with distant metastases → no influence on survival
segmental hepatic resection
biliary

two hepatic ducts

  • Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma
  • Only curative intent
  • Resection of affected biliary tract + liver resection
  • Frequently, parts of liver, gall bladder and local lymph nodes and parts of intestine and pancreas resected
  • Restoration of bile flow by anastomosis of biliary stump to intestinal loop (hepato-jejunal anastomosis)
Bismuth Iwithout hepatectomy
Bismuth IIresection of bile ducts with segment I
Bismuth IIIright/ left hepatectomy with segment I
Bismuth IVdrainage
  • Distal cholangiocarcinoma
  • Resection of tumor localized distally on common bile duct + resection of duodenum and pancreatic head = Whipple (block resection of main bile duct, gallbladder, duodenum, antrum of stomach and head of pancreas + anastomosis of cephalic portion of pancreas to stomach or jejunum, gastro jejunal and hepatico jejunal anastomosis) = Traverso Longmire → variant of this intervention with preservation of pylorus

b. & c. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy

  • Role not well defined
  • Might have benefit in survival time → chemotherapy + surgery + radiotherapy

d. Palliative treatment

  • To establish continuity of biliary tree and to maintain bile flow
  • Intrahepatic type - percutaneous external hepatic drainage placed under ultrasound guidance, benefit from tumor

ablation procedures and chemoembolization

  • Extrahepatic tumors - placing stents through ERCP or by performing biliary digestive anastomosis upstream

The gallbladder and bileducts Benign biliary disorders

Gallbladder lithiasis

Marius Stanca

Learning objectives:

  • To know the lithiasic pathology of the gallbladder and its complications.
  • To know the principles of treatment in gallstones pathology.

Relevant anatomy of the biliary tree

Extrahepatic biliary tree consist of common bile duct (CBD) and a diverticulum, the gallbladder, connected by a tortuous duct, named the cystic duct.

Into the liver parenchyma, on both sides, right and left, the intrahepatic bile ducts converge, forming in the end two main bile ducts, the right hepatic duct, which is draining the right liver, and the left hepatic duct, which is draining the left liver. This two have a more or less path inside the liver and meet together outside the parenchyma, forming the common bile duct. From the hepatic junction, the CBD is travelling downwards, along the portal vein and proper hepatic artery, heading the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum, crossing the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum, the posterior face of the head of the pancreas and, finally, entering into the pancreas parenchyma and joining the Wirsung duct and then the duodenum. There are described three sections of the CBD, the supraduodenal, retroduodenal and intrapancreatic, the latter including also the vatero-oddian part. Normal sizes of the CBD are approximately 10-12cm in length and 7-10mm in diameter.

Fig.36:Gallblader and main bile duct anatomy

The gallbladder is a diverticulum of the CBD it is situated on the inferior face of the segment V of the liver. It is pear- shaped, with its fundus reaching the anterior liver margin, the body and the infundibulum heading posterior, towards CBD. It is continued by the cystic duct. The cystic duct is approaching the CBD in the supraduodenal region, but usually is travelling along the CBD for about 1 cm, the actual junction being located right above the duodenum or, sometimes in the retroduodenal part of the CBD. It is described the cholecystectomy triangle, a.k.a. Calot triangle, formed by the cystic duct, the right side of the CBD and the inferior face of the liver, which is crossed by the cystic artery, originated from the right hepatic artery. Gallbladder’s veins are draining directly into the intrahepatic portal branches (fig.36).

Biliary physiology

Bile represents the main exocrine liver secretion. Produced by the hepatocytes, its secretion is unceasing, with a mean physiological flow of 1ml/minute (maximum 10-12ml/min during meals), reaching an amount of 1000-1500ml a day. The normal bile pressure is of 9-10cmH2O in CBD, 8-10cmH2O in gallbladder. In contraction, the gallbladder pressure increases to 14-18cm H2O and during colic can reach 25cmH2O. Comparing with blood pressure, the bile’s is low, which, in presence of any disturbance, predispose to stasis. The constituents of the bile are water mixed with cholesterol, phospholipids (lecithin), bile salts (mainly chenodeoxicholic and cholic acid) and conjugated bilirubin (the breakdown product of haemoglobin). Cholesterol is not water soluble, so it is mixing with phospholipids and bile salts, forming water-soluble micelles. The colloidal stability of the cholesterol is depending on phospholipids and bile salts concentration, when the proportion of the bile constituents is unbiased, the bile becomes lithogenic, meaning the cholesterol will crystallize, starting the process of stone formation.

Between meals, the sphincter of Oddi is closed and the bile secretion is accumulating into the gallbladder, where is concentrated by water absorption. During meals, under the neuro-hormonal influences (parasimpatic, cholecystikinin, acid pH), the gallbladder will contract and will push its content, via common bile duct and sphincter of Oddi into the duodenum. In the small intestine, the bile is acting as a detergent, emulsifying the fats to facilitate their digestion. The bile salts and pigments are resorbed in the distal gut and via portal venous system will pass back into the liver, where will be secreted into the bile again. This mechanism is called enterohepatic circulation. The absence of the distal small bowel (i.e. resection of distal ileum) will interrupt this circulation, reducing the quantity of bile salts in the bile. This unbiases the cholesterol concentration, making the bile lithogenic. Absence of the bile in the intestine (external bile drainage, obstructive jaundice) results in a malabsorption of fats, fat-soluble vitamins (A,D,E,K), alteration of intestinal microbial flora and impairment of the intestinal wall trophicity.

Gallbladder lithiasis and its complications

Stone formation is a complex process which implies a lithogenic bile and an alteration of the gallbladder (functional or anatomical), which fosters the concentration and stasis of the lithogenic bile. The bile becomes lithogenic when either the concentration of cholesterol rises or the concentration of the bile salts and lecithin decreases. Lithogenesis go through 3 stages: a) chemical stage – in which appears the lithogenic bile;b) physical stage, in which the cholesterol is crystallizing, the microcrystals gathering around mucine and glicoproteins and c) lithogenesis in fact, when the cholesterol precipitates and accumulates around nucleus formed by the mucine, dead bacteria, desquamated epithelia.

There are three types of gallstones: cholesterol stones, pigment stones and mixed stones.

Cholesterol stones (20%) occur either as a solitary, oval stone, or as multiple calculi of different sizes, one indenting the other. It is not proved the high levels of blood cholesterol can be considered as a risk factor, but there is a definite correlation between this stones and pregnancy, contraceptive pill, family history, obesity, low dietary fibre.

Pigment stones (5%) are irregular, black and small in size, sometimes looking as covered with thorns, are composed of calcium bilirubinate and carbonate. They occur in haemolytic anaemia, when is a superproduction of haemoglobin and its breakdown products.

Mixed stones (75%) are the most common. Varying in size, shape and colour, are formed by a mix of cholesterol and bile pigments.

Although there is this classification into three groups of calculi, based on their chemical constituents, in reality all forms of gallstones represent different combinations of the same ingredients.

Clinical features of the gallstones.

Although in about 80% of cases the stones are silent, meaning that the patient is symptom free, in the rest the disease is manifesting by its most characteristic syndrome – the biliary colic, or by the complication. Sometimes patients with stones accuse a plethora of symptoms, which are not always caused by the disease itself: migraine, headache, nausea, vomiting, and a dull pain in the epigastrum or right abdominal quadrant. Other times it can manifest by an episode of acute pancreatitis.

The biliary colic is the one that features the best the presence of the gallstones. It occurs when the cholecyst is contracting against an obstacle, which is represented by a stone impacted either in the Hartmann’s pouch or in the cystic duct, obstructing the outflow of the bile into the choledoc. The pain is generated by the violent and sustained contraction of the gallbladder’s wall and distension. The pain is occurring usually after 2-3 hours after a meal in the right hypocondrum or epigastrum, is severe in intensity, increases progressively, reaching a plateau, lasting then for several hours. Backwards radiation to the inferior angle of the scapula is common. Additionally nausea, vomiting and sweating are present in most of the cases. The patient tends to lie still, but the general status is not systematically unwell.

The differential diagnostic is made with other causes of acute, severe pain, such as renal colic, peptic ulcer, appendicular colic etc.

Complications of the gallbladder lithiasis

During contractions of the gallbladder, the stones are pushed towards the cystic duct and, depending on their size, they can get impacted at different levels of the biliary tree, usually the narrow parts (infundibulum, cystic duct, sphincter of Oddi), or they can freely pass into the duodenum (if small enough). Blockage of the stone (which can be assumed as a mechanical complication) is followed by a local inflammatory response and its consequences (inflammatory complication). Another type of complication occurs as a result of the chronic inflammation caused by large, heavy stones, which leads to dysplasia and, in the end, to neoplasia (degenerative complication).

Acute cholecystitis

After the impaction of a stone into the infundibulum or cystic duct, the concentrated bile will irritate the mucosa of the gallbladder, expressed by an inflamed wall (as a chemical cholecystitis). First, the content is sterile, and then becomes infected. In evolution, the gallbladder wall will pass through all stages of inflammation, starting with catarrhal and finishing with gangrenous. These changes translate in a persistent and intense pain in the right hypocondrum, accompanied by high fever, in the range of 38-39˚C, with marked toxaemia. The pain last for hours, nausea and vomiting are common. Palpation of the upper abdomen reveals tenderness, even contraction in severe cases. Murphy sign is positive. Sometimes there is a palpable painful mass in the right hypochondrum, which is caused by the distended inflamed cholecyst, blocked by and wrapped in the inflammatory adhesions to adjacent organs, especially the great omentum, duodenum and colon (subhepatic block).

Under the treatment or spontaneously, the stone falls back into the gallbladder and the evolution is to restoration, but the recurrence it’s almost a rule. In other situations, if the stone is impacted into the cystic duct, the cholecyst mucosa will reabsorb the biliar pigments and secrete an appreciable amount of mucus. The gallbladder appears distended, in tension, palpable and the content is clear, transparent and uncolored – hydrocholecyst.

In case of large stones, rarely the swollen gallbladder can press against the common bile duct, producing obstructive jaundice, but normally this occurs as a result of a long local inflammation (the Mirrizzi syndrome).

Seldom a gallbladder empyema occurs, but rarely perforates into the general peritoneal cavity. Usually, the later complication concerns old immune impaired patients. In rest of the patients, progression of the inflammation being slow, the perforation takes place into the subhepatic block. As a result, the patient will present a subhepatic abscess, with a severe infectious syndrome.

The differential diagnosis is from other diseases that evolve with intense pain in the right hypochondrum: perforated peptic ulcer, acute pancreatitis, acute appendicitis, acute hepatitis, right sided basal pneumonia or inferior wall coronary accident. When there is a subhepatic block, one considers different tumours in the area, or hypertrophy of liver segments.

Chronic cholecystitis

Although almost all of the specimens removed by cholecystectomy are labelled “chronic cholecystitis”, this name should be attributed only in those cases in which, after repeated episodes of inflammatory attacks, the gallbladder’s wall become rigid, fibrotic, more often being moulded on calculi (scleroatrophic cholecystitis), or having a thick, hypertrophied wall (sclerohypertrophic cholecystitis). The bile content is or not infected.

Chronic cholecystitis is featured by recurrent bouts of abdominal pain, bearing even a mild cholecystitis aspect, but usually without fever. Fatty meals are followed by abdominal discomfort and flatulence. Over these aspects, attacks of acute cholecystitis can occur.

The differential diagnosis comprises other causes of chronic dyspepsia, such as peptic ulcer, hiatus hernia, but the symptoms can mimic coronary insufficiency too.

In 15-20% of cases, gallbladder lithiasis can be complicated by the migration of the stones into the common bile duct. In only a few situations, the CBD lithiasis can originate from the choledoc itself, or from the intrahepatic ducts (i.e. Caroli disease, inflammatory bile duct stenosis). Depending on the size of calculi, this can pass through the sphincter of Oddi into the duodenum, or can get stuck at the level of the Vater’s ampula, generating upwards distension and biliary obstruction. The blockage is translated clinical by severe pain, accompanied by chills or fever and, if the obstruction last enough, jaundice.

The most distinctive form of manifestation of the CBD stones is the major choledochal syndrome, or Charcot triad:Pain (intense, backward radiated) followed by fever and, after 12-24 hours, jaundice. The sudden distension of the CBD is causing pain, fever is a result of angiocholitis. After 12-24h of biliary stasis, due to the increased pressure inside the bile ducts, the hepatocytes will change their secretor polarity and the bile will be regurgitated into the blood, manifested by jaundice.The attack ceases when the stone is pushed by pressure through the sphincter of Oddi, or the stone disimpacts and falls back into dilated CBD. In the latter situation, the stone can impact again at any time, with the same consequences.

The typical form of Charcot triad is encountered only in half of cases. The rest of cases present concealed forms, usually missing intense jaundice. The patients can accuse a minor choledochal syndrome (pain, chills, and dark urines after colic), feverish forms with toxaemia (the intermittent hepatic fever of Charcot), dyspepsia.

The presence of stones in the common bile duct, even when is not completely obstructive, it produces a certain degree of stenosis, leading to increase in bile pressure, reverberated on the hepatocytes. If the CBD is not freed from stones, the chronic bile back-pressure, on which repeated episodes of cholangitis are added, may result in liver fibrosis and inflammation – secondary biliary cirrhosis.

In the presence of jaundice, the differential diagnosis is made with hepatic jaundice (acute hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug related cholestasis, liver poisoning, liver tumors), or posthepatic jaundice caused by other conditions than stones (congenital and postraumatic strictures, sclerosing cholangitis, bile duct tumors, external compression made by periampulary tumors, pancreatitis, hilar limphadenopathy). In forms without jaundice, the differential is led by pain: peptic ulcer, renal colic, intestinal obstruction, angina pectoris. Acute pancreatitis is of peculiar importance, because it can mimic CBD stones, but it can be, as well, caused by them.

Spontaneous bilio-biliary fistulas

These represent another gallstones complication. Commonly there are two types of internal fistulas: intrabiliar fistulas and biliary-gastrointestinal fistulas. The producing mechanism is complex and long. In an obstructive acute cholecystitis, the constant increasing pressure inside the gallbladder causes ischemia of the wall, with focal necrosis. First, this will lead to adhesions to the neighboring elements of the biliary tree. In time, these adhesions becomeprogressively tighter, the fibrosis raising the pressure between the gallbladder’s wall and the main bile duct.The duration of biliary symptoms prior to identification of a fistula ranges from 8 to 20 years.

Intrabiliary fistulas

Consistof an abnormal communication between the gallbladder and other segments of the biliary tree, usually the CBD (or the right hepatic duct). Essentially, finally all patients will have choledocholithiasis due to transfistular migration of the gallbladder calculi.

Laboratory work-up of gallstones

In absence of any of its complication, gallbladder lithiasis reveals normal lab tests. Complete blood count and liver function tests are commonly performed.

Leukocytosis features the inflammatory and infectious complication of the gallbladder and the biliary tree. Usually ranges between 10 and 16 000/mmc, values higher than this suggesting empyema of the cholecyst or a severe cholangitis.

Prothrombintime should be checked in every surgical patient, but especially in those with prolonged jaundice. Due to the lack of bile in the gut, the absorption of vitamin K is impaired. More, prolonged coagulation time could be a sign of liver failure as well.

Bilirubin (total and conjugated) is raised in obstructive jaundice.Right above the normal levels can be encountered in severe acute cholecystitis, without meaning of a biliary obstruction. After releasing of an obstacle in the CBD, the levels of bilirubin should drop to normal, otherwise it suggests incomplete procedure.

Alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamil-transpeptidase are tests of cholestasis, meaning retention of bile acids into the hepatocytes. Posthepatic cholestasis occurs every time there is a stenosis in the biliary tree. These two enzymes are raising together, if no, other conditions than cholestasis should be investigated. 5-nucleotidase is a more sensible marker of cholestasis.

Transaminases (ASAT, ALAT) are signs of hepatocytolisis and in absence of a concomitant hepatic disease, it react in specific condition, such as severe cholecystitis and cholangitis.

Imaging tests in gallstones disease

Plain abdominal X-ray is not a reliable imaging test for gallbladder lithiasis, hence less than 10% of stones are radio-opaque. Occasionally, a calcified cholecyst can be seen (‘porcelain gallbladder’). Image of gas in the bile ducts is a sign of communication between biliary tree and gastrointestinal tract, meaning a biliary fistula. This aspect appears normally after bilio-digestive anastomosis, or endoscopic instrumentation of the CBD.

Ultrasound plays a key role in biliary investigation. Apart of being cheap and almost ubiquitous, ultrasonography is important because it offers three fields of information: a)the presence of the gallstones (intense echogenic foci which cast an important acoustic shadow beyond them); b) the thickened wall of cholecyst in inflammatory condition (typical image of acute cholecystitis is of gallbladder double wall offered by the echogenic layer of serosa and mucosa, separated by oedema, which appears hypoechogenic); c)it measures the diameter of the common bile duct, if above 7mm suggesting a stenosis or the presence of CBD lithiasis. More, it can appreciate the liver parenchyma and the pancreas. In jaundice, measuring the bile ducts, ultrasonography offers a clue about existence or non-existence of an obstruction. Unfortunately, ultrasonography is not the test of choice in detecting CBD lithiasis, especially for stones located in the lower part of the choledoc, because stones are obscured by the duodenal gas.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography ERCP is a maneuver by which the choledoc is endoscopic intubated and filled with radiological contrast through the ampulla of Vater for obtaining the radiological image of bile and pancreatic ducts. It allows the endoscopist to perform a sphincterotomy and then, the instrumentation of the CBD. By this way, one can remove stones or insert stents. Because is an invasive procedure, carrying the burden of severe complication (acute pancreatitis, perforation of ducts, peritonitis, bleeding, allergy to contrast), ERCP is not used anymore just for diagnostic purposes, but remains a valuable therapeutic tool in hepato-biliary management, removing the reliance only on surgical procedures.

Magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography MRCP is offering the visualisation of the biliary tree and its diseases, stones included. This is a non-invasive procedure, it gives the same diagnostic information as ERCP without the risks of the latter, but provides imaging information about the rest of the abdominal viscera. The drawback of the method is the lack of any therapeutic possibilities.

Treatment of the gallstones and their complications

A proportion of 20% of population is gallstone carrier, but only one in five of those are symptomatic. From the moment the gallbladder lithiasis start to manifest, a therapeutic approach should consider, because further attacks are more likely, and the risk of development of a complication is raising in time.

There are two options in treating gallstones: by surgery or by medication.

Despite the fact that patients, generally, are reluctant to surgery, and they would prefer a conservative cure, using medication for dissolving the stones is not only a method with high rates of failure, but can be even dangerous. Drugs are bile acid based (ursodeoxycholic acid) and act by changing the chemical composition of the bile, reversing the process of cholesterol crystallisation in dissolution. This treatment is of a life time duration, it takes months or years to dissolve a stone, sometimes don’t work and, if stopped, the recurrence of stones is a rule. More of that, decreasing the size of the stones, makes them susceptible to migrate into the common bile duct, with all of its consequences. For these reasons, medical treatment of gallstones is reserved for those who reject surgery or who are not suitable for it because of other important, life-threatening comorbidities.

Surgical treatment of gallbladder lithiasis consists mainly incholecystectomy (surgical removal of the gallbladder). The approach was open (“classic”), by laparotomy, till the arising of laparoscopy (“the new classic”) which, in absence of counter indications, is the only accepted approach. Irrespective of the way of doing it, the steps the surgeon follows are the same: dissection, ligation and section of the cystic duct and cystic artery in the Calot triangle (delineated by cystic duct, right border of CBD and the liver surface) and dissection of the gallbladder from its liver fossa. If the dissection progress from the cystic towards the fundus, it is called retrograde cholecystectomy,and if removal starts fundus first (fig.37);anterograde cholecystectomy (direction from or towards pedicle of gallbladder names the technique).

Cholecystostomy is a minimal invasive technique by which the surgeon performs a connection between the gallbladder and exterior, extracting the stones and draining outside the bile liquid.Its role is to decompress the cholecyst in patients with important comorbidities, unsuitable for general anaesthesia. Cholecystectomy as a second time is required.

Special situations

The symptomless gallstone. Still in debate, the symptomless gallstone patient is a clinical challenge. Raging from the clear indication for cholecystectomy at the time of diagnosis, in order to avoid possible complications, to total surgical abstinence, the attitude in front of this situation is not clearly defined and it depends on surgical school and tradition. Long-term follow-up studies are shown that most of the patient will remain asymptomatic, and the prophylactic cholecystectomy is not generally recommended for prevention of the gallbladder cancer. However, there are some instances when cholecystectomy is advisable because of the risk of developing complications: young patient with large stones, haemolytic stones, and transplant recipients.

Acute cholecystitis.Surgery is the best option for acute cholecystitis, but the emergency degree depends on the presence of the signs of gravity. In the past it was believed that “chilling-out” inflammatory process before intervention is mandatory, in order to avoid operating on inflamed tissues, with important bleeding and risk of iatrogenic lesions. For that, the patient was put in hospital bed, with intravenous hydration, broad spectrum antibiotics, antiinflammatory drugs and a bag of ice on the right hypocondrum. Cholecystectomy was due to perform after 7-10 days of medical treatment. Large studies showed this attitude proved to be redundant and risky, because the intervention is done on fibrotic tissue and anatomical post-inflammatory changes.

In the present days, the intervention is done in the first 24-72 hours after the onset of cholecystitis. Prior the intervention, the patient is administrated iv hydration, broad spectrum antibiotics (methronidasole and a peniciline or aminoglycoside), antispastics and antialgics. Though the procedure is performed in full process of inflammation, the bleeding is not that important and the oedema in the gallbladder’s wall facilitates dissection. Extraction of the infected cholecyst should be done in a plastic bag, to protect the abdominal wall from suppuration. Even in cases of subhepatic block, gentle and careful blunt dissection safely disrupt inflammatory adhesions and the surgical intervention can successful be done.After the operation the antibiotherapy is no longer required.

Biliary fistulas. Biliary-digestive fistula requires two types of intervention: cholecystectomy and repairing of the digestive tract. Usually performed by open approach, these interventions could be done by laparoscopy. In cases of intestinal obstruction caused by large impacted stones, removal of lithiasic obstacle from the gut is needed.

Intrabiliary fistulas are a challenging situation due to the complex destruction of the common bile duct or of the right hepatic duct. More, the Calot triangle is severely modified, raising the risk of vascular lesions. Exact diagnosis and a complete mapping of biliary tract before the intervention is mandatory, but sometimes this complication is an intraoperatory discovery. The best solution to resolve the complication is to perform a cholecystectomy and a biliary repair, by a Roux-en Y hepatico-jejunostomy.

ANATOMY OF THE MAIN BILE DUCT (MBD)

The main bile duct occupies the subhepatic space, situated to the right of the supramesocolic abdominal compartment, delimited anterosuperiorly by the visceral side of the liver and inferiorly by the transverse mesocolon. It consists of thecommon hepatic duct and the common bile duct.

  • The common hepatic duct (CHD) arises from the hepatic hilum through the convergence of the right and left hepatic ducts. It is situated in the free margin of the hepatoduodenal ligament, where it descends ventrally to the portal vein, to the right of the proper hepatic artery. It has a 3-4 cm length and a 5 mm caliber.
  • The common bile duct (CBD) continues the common hepatic duct and extends from its junction with the cystic duct to the duodenum. It has a length of 5-6 cm. It is divided into four segments: supraduodenal, retroduodenal, pancreatic and intraparietal. The supraduodenal segment (situated between the cystic duct-common hepatic duct junction and the upper margin of the duodenum) extends between the layers of the free margin of the lesser omentum (the hepatoduodenal ligament) together with the two other pedicular elements (the portal vein – posteriorly and the proper hepatic artery to the left). (fig.36)

The retropancreatic segment projects (together with the main pancreatic duct) at the level of the abdominal wall in Chauffard’s choledochopancreatic zone (between the median vertical and the horizontal passing through the umbilicus, a right angle open to the right is formed; between the bisector of this angle and the vertical – 5 cm – this choledochopancreatic zone is delimited). At this level, pain in choledochal colic is projected.

The arterial blood supply of the hepatocholedochal duct is derived from five sources: the right hepatic artery, the proper hepatic artery, the cystic artery, the gastroduodenal artery and the retroduodenal artery, which contribute to the formation of the epicholedochal arterial plexus. Ensuring a well vascularized biliary stump is of great importance in the trophicity of biliodigestive anastomoses.

INTRODUCTION

Known since ancient pre-Christian times, gallstones represent one of the serious public health problems today. The 20 million cases treated annually in USA alone incur a cost of about 6.2 billion dollars to the system.

The second most frequent complication of gallbladder stones (GS), common bile duct stones (CBDS) have many interesting clinical-evolutive, diagnostic and therapeutic particularities. These, together with specific complications (frequently dreadful, with lethal potential) justify the distinct approach of this condition as part of cholelithiasis.

Frequency. In Europe and USA, gallbladder stones affect about 10-15% of the population, and CBD stones are present in 10-20% of all cases diagnosed with cholecystolithiasis.

Necropsy studies have evidenced CBD stones in 24% of all cases with cholelithiasis.

Certainly, there are ethnic and geographic variations.

RISK FACTORS

For secondary common bile duct stones (by migration), risk factors are as follows: 1. Small size gallbladder stones (3-5 mm); 2. A large cystic duct; 3. A gallbladder with contractile walls; 4. Cystic duct stones (residual stones after cholecystectomy), in a cystic duct with a

particular appearance, the so-called “double-barrel shotgun sign”, which runs

parallel to the common bile duct, into which it inserts retroduodenally or even

retropancreatically. In this situation, intracystic calculi are not recognized

intraoperatively; they are residual calculi. They can “supply” recurrent choledochal

migration episodes (recurrent choledocholithiasis); 5. Another risk factor is the long evolution of cholecystolithiasis. The longer its natural

history, the higher the risk of migration to the common bile duct. Thus, while 10-20

of 100 cholecystectomized patients (for gallbladder stones) can concomitantly have

(migrated) common bile duct stones, in the case of patients carrying gallbladder

calculi for more than 20 years, the risk of migration increases seven times.

For primary common bile duct stones (calculi formed in the common bile duct), the risk factors are: 1. Sclerosing cholangitis; 2. Parasitic infection (Clonorchis sinensis); 3. Stenosis of the biliary tree; 4. Caroli disease; 5. Benign stenosis of the sphincter of Oddi; 6. Mirizzi syndrome type I.

THE ORIGIN OF COMMON BILE DUCT STONES

From the point of view of their origin, common bile duct stones can be primary and migrated:

1. Primary common bile duct stones are rare (4%). They occur only when favorable conditions are created for their formation in the CBD. Of these, bile stasis is an indispensable element. Both in Europe and USA, chronic cephalic pancreatitis, sclerosing odditis, (iatrogenic) post-traumatic common bile duct stenoses are the most frequent causes.

Once stenosis has established, infection and inflammation occur. The excess germs developed will release beta-glucuronidase; this will deconjugate conjugated bilirubin (normally present in the biliary tree), resulting in unconjugated bilirubin, which characteristically precipitates easily. Thus, pigment calculi are formed.

In other geographical regions (Far East, Asia), the main etiological factor is the frequent infection of the biliary tree with parasites (Fasciola hepatica, Clonorchis sinensis). These induce biliary epithelial lesions that will heal by fibrosis, generating segmental biliary stenoses, both intra- and extrahepatic. From this point onwards, the mechanisms are similar to those already described, i.e., lithogenesis on this favorable background (stenosis, bile stasis) will start only after bacterial superinfection (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella), which will initiate the known pathogenic sequence: beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin → precipitation → sludge → (calcium bilirubinate and pigment) stones.

There is a category of primary common bile duct stones that can form right above the ampulla of Vater, even in the presence of a permeable (but rigid, sclerosing) papilla, with a dilated superjacent choledochus. They have a typically ovoid appearance, a brown-yellow color and the crumbly consistency of dry modeling clay.
