2. Migrated common bile duct stones – are the most frequent ones. Regarding their origin, the finding that “95% of patients with choledocholithiasis also have gall bladder lithiasis” (Pascu) is extremely suggestive. The main source of migrated common bile duct stones is indeed the lithiasic gallbladder.

A contractile gallbladder (contraction triggered by a cholecystokinetic meal), small/medium sized calculi, a large or enlarged cystic duct, as well as intraoperative procedures (e.g., elongation – verticalization of the gallbladder with the fundus grasping forceps during laparoscopic cholecystectomy – “turning the bottle upside down”) are factors favoring or triggering stones’ migration.

Characteristically, migrated common bile duct stones have the same gross appearance and composition as the gallbladder ones: blackberry-like or facetted, hard, predominantly consisting of cholesterin (unlike primary stones, which have poor cholesterin content).

Above we described migration “by natural route”, normal migration that occurs through the only anatomical cholecystocholedochal connection, i.e., the cystic duct. For old and large gallbladder calculi, impacted in the infundibulum or in Hartmann’s pouch, there is another possibility of migration, an aberrant one. Since the cystic duct caliber is obviously too small to allow the migration of a heavy, large stone, this will slowly and progressively build, during the course of years, an abnormal direct connection with the common bile duct; this is achieved by the exertion of a continuous mechanical pressure on the “funnel” of the cystic duct, which is continuously compressed up to its destruction (along its long axis). In time, the cystic duct will be progressively squeezed, shortened and dilated and finally transformed in an orifice, a fistula, between the gallbladder and the main bile duct, i.e., a cholecysto-choledochal fistula; the same continuous compression will gradually enlarge this orifice, resulting in the projection of the calculus in the lumen of the common bile duct.

This constant erosive progression can be compared to the slow, continuously eroding movement of a mountain glacier. Also, the abnormal enlargement of the cystic orifice is similar to the unexpectedly great dilation of the pharynx of a snake swallowing a prey with a much larger diameter.

When up to 1/3 of the common bile duct caliber has been eroded, Mirizzi syndrome type II (Mc Sherry) occurs. Subsequently, the cholecystocholedochal fistula can enlarge (up to 2/3 of the common bile duct caliber) = Mirizzi syndrome type III; the complete destruction of the common bile duct caliber = Mirizzi syndrome type IV – Csendes-1989. In this way, a disproportionately larger stone compared to the cystic duct and even to the common bile duct can “herniate” into the CBD lumen, partially or completely obstructing the bile flow.

(Just as a reminder, Mirizzi syndrome, type I, consists of an extrinsic compression of the main bile duct by the adjacent dilated Hartman’s pouch, filled with a large, heavy stone).

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

- Choledocholithiasis by migration:

Regardless of the origin of the stones, once migrated in the common bile duct, they will establish and accumulate mainly in its terminal (ampullary) segment. Basically, the pathophysiology of choledocholithiasis is governed by Bergman’s triad: calculus migrated in the common bile duct → bile stasis (cholestasis) → superinfection (cholangitis). Obviously, the phenomenon is more complex and requires refined explanations. In the first place, it should be understood that the intensity, the severity of loco-regional and subsequently systemic consequences depends not only on the characteristics of the migrated stones, but also, to a very large extent, on the response of the local (sphincter of Oddi, extrahepatic bile ducts) and regional anatomic structures (liver, pancreas) respectively, to these “migrated stone’s mechanical aggression”.

Thus, small stones (5-7 mm in diameter) can spontaneously migrate through a permeable cystic duct, possibly driven by the gallbladder contractions triggered by a cholecystokinetic meal, into the CBD. Once having reached the sphincter of Oddi, they generate a reflex prolonged spasm, thus becoming obstructive. Stasis and subsequently, upstream intrabiliary hyperpressure develop.

Spasm and hyperpressure with consequent sudden dilation of the extrahepatic biliary tree, will clinically translate into pain(choledochal colic) and biliary stasis, which, if lasting long enough, into superinfection (chills, fever). However, sphincter spasm can frequently be relieved (spontaneously or therapeutically); the papilla opens and under upstream biliary pressure, the stones are discharged into the duodenum, with the disappearance of all clinical consequences.

Larger calculi, 10-15 mm in size, having reached the choledochus (through a more enlarged cystic duct), may cause similar phenomena, but for a longer duration and with a higher intensity. Even if initially, the lithiasic obstruction can be incomplete, the mechanical/chemical irritation caused in the terminal common bile duct generates, in addition to persistent oddian sphincteric spasm, local edema/inflammation, which completes the obstruction. Given that the liver (hepatocytes) continues to produce and excrete bile, the result will be the progressive distension, dilation of the extrahepatic bile ducts (EHBD); pressure will continue to increase, up to the mechanical limits beyond which, bile excretion at the hepatocyte biliary side will stop; from this moment onwards, bile will regurgitate upstream through the perihepatocytary spaces, and even through the hepatocytes, towards the opposite side, the vascular one, into the sinusoidal capillaries, thus generating the third major clinical sign, thejaundice.

With the relaxation of the oddian sphincter’s spasm, larger stones, even if not discharged into the duodenum, can “fall back” into the common bile duct, disobstructing temporarily the papilla. Thisalternationof active clinical phenomena with periods of lull is a characteristic clinical feature ofcholedocholithiasis; the common bile duct stones that generate this clinical picture are termed “floating” stones. However, in time, repeated trans-papillary passages as well as the prolonged presence, even if non-obstructive, of the stones in the common bile duct will generate repeated acute inflammatory episodes. In time, these will evolve towards chronic inflammation, with permanent sclerosis/fibrosis. Hence, a benign stenosis of the papilla may occur (a rare condition), together with a so-called chronic pediculitis(thickened, inflamed CBD walls, generating strong adhesions to the adjacent portal vein and hepatic artery, creating technical difficulties during surgical dissection).

A paradoxical variant is the so-called common bile duct “rock paving”; this consists of the accumulation of many calculi in the common bile duct (sometimes tens or hundreds). The paradoxical element is frequently the fact that these forms evolve without manifest jaundice, the bile flowing like “the river water through rocks”. The stones can sometimes fill-up the entire extra-hepatic biliary tree.

However, there are also situations when a (usually larger) stone remains trapped, irreversibly impacted, in the papilla or the terminal common bile duct; clinical phenomena can be noisy (acute papillary obstruction), with pain and jaundice, of progressively increasing intensity up to persistent, constant (not variable) “icterus melas”, this time resembling the clinical features of a malignant biliary obstruction.

The consequences of the presence of calculi in the common bile duct extend in time from a local to a regional level; the liver is among the first affected organs. Cholestasis is frequently accompanied by hepatocytolysis, which can be marked, resulting in the so-called –“satellite hepatitis”.

The second important affected organ, sometimes with dramatic consequences, is the pancreas. Acute biliary pancreatitis, generated particularly by the migration of small calculi (smaller than 5 mm), is well known (ampullary impaction of a stone, especially distal to the bilio-pancreatic confluence, with consequent regurgitation of bile into the Wirsung duct and local activation of the pancreatic enzymes!).

Repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis or just repeated pancreatic reactions generated by recurrent small stones’ passages, can lead, in time, to the progressive development of a chronic biliary pancreatitis, with potential consecutive distal choledochal stenosis, and pancreatic exo- and endocrine insufficiency.

DIAGNOSIS

1. Clinical diagnosis

The clinical forms of choledocho-lithiasis cover a wide spectrum, from the acute, violent cholangitic form, with hepato-renal failure (particularly severe), to the completely asymptomatic silent and clinically mute form.

  • In the classic, complete clinical form (40-50% of cases), all three

semiological elements of the Villard’s triad (later attributed to Charcot) are present: pain, fever, jaundice. This order is not aleatory, as this is the specific order of their appearance.

Onset can be sudden, in full health (previously asymptomatic carriers of gallbladder stones), or progressive, in the sense that the initial acute episode of choledochal migration occurs after months or even years of repeated biliary colics.

Pain, the most frequent symptom, is classically described as very intense, sharp, with sudden onset, 4-6 hours after ingestion of a cholecystokinetic meal; intensity rapidly becomes paroxysmal and is maintained at a plateau level for minutes, hours or even days. It is typically located in the right upper quadrant and epigastric (Chauffard’s choledochopancreatic zone), with possible irradiation to the left upper quadrant and left supraclavicular area (pancreatic type); it is exacerbated by palpation and mobilization.

Fever occurs after several hours and is characteristically preceded by chills; it is the consequence of sepsis with a biliary starting point (cholangitis). Unlike acute cholecystitis, in this cases the fever curve has great oscillations and higher values (39-40˚C) and can last for days or until biliary drainage – spontaneous (with the migration of obstructive calculi to the duodenum) or therapeutic.

Jaundice characteristically develops 24-48 hours after the initial colic; it is of moderate intensity and typically, has an intermittent appearance; when persistent, it is of variable intensity (fluctuating jaundice), painful and febrile. There may be spontaneous remissions (sometimes long-lasting – calculus eliminated through the papilla of Vater, at other times for a short period – calculus mobilized from the papilla in cranial direction, migrating upstream, subsequently returning to the papilla).

In terms of color, lithiasic jaundice is yellow red/greenish. Only in pseudoneoplastic forms (fixed, completely obstructing, impacted intrapapillary stone), with a long evolution, can the typically neoplastic icterus melas color develop. However, in general, lithiasic jaundice does never reach the intensity of the one generated by a malignant biliary obstruction.

It should be mentioned that forms with prolonged, neglected and intense cholestasis, can be accompanied by pruritus, which is sometimes refractory and difficult to control (before the cause is solved). Characteristically, pruritus in choledocholithiasis develops only (long) after the onset of jaundice, while in neoplastic biliary obstructions, pruritus may precede jaundice even by weeks!

2. Laboratory tests:

Total hyperbilirubinemia, with the predominance of direct hyperbilirubinemia, occurs in the vast majority of the cases. Characteristically, serum total bilirubin levels rarely exceed 15 mg/dl (except for the neoplasic-like forms), as biliary main bile duct stones most frequently generate an incomplete and intermittent obstruction.

Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase values may increase before the bilirubin ones; after removal of the biliary obstruction, they decrease progressively.

Serum transaminases’ levels can rarely be increased, when cholestasis is prolonged, determining cytolysis. Very rarely however, values can increase up to ones mimicking acute viral hepatitis (1000 – 2000 UI/L); in lithiasis, these are rapidly restored to normal (withindays), while in hepatitis, regression lasts for weeks. Prolonged absence of bile from the digestive tract (in tight and persistent obstructions) can lead to vitamin K malabsorption and secondarily, to a state of hypocoagulability due to the absence of coagulating factors, synthesized by the hepatocytes only in the presence of vitamin K (factors II, VII, IX, X); vitamin K administration will correct coagulability (prothrombin index – positive Koller’s test). In patients with liver insufficiency (chronic hepatic diseases, cirrhoses), the Koller’s test is negative (vitamin K will not significantly improve coagulation, i.e. the prothrombin index!).

Renal function should be carefully monitored in patients with choledocholithiasis, due to a serious risk for toxaemic concomitant renal failure!).

Serum and urine amylases are also important for monitoring or for evidencing a pancreatic reaction or even acute pancreatitis, which can also occur in choledocholithiasis.

6. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)(fig.42)

After visualizing the papilla with a duodenoscope (lateral-view endoscope), its canulation is performed using a catheter (introduced through the working channel).

Through this, the contrast product is intraductally injected, and the retrograde radiological opacification of the bile ducts (cholangiography) and pancreatic ducts (pancreatography) is achieved. The obtained images are highly accurate.

Due to its high sensitivity (97%) and specificity (100%) in detecting common bile duct stones, ERCP is still considered the reference technique for the contrast-enhanced radiological exploration of the bile ducts.

Being an invasive examination, ERCP can generate complications; these occur with a frequency inversely proportional to the endoscopist’s experience.

Intraoperative exploration of the CBD

Regardless of the surgical approach (laparoscopic or open), the intraoperative imaging exploration of the bile ducts benefits from three methods that complement one another:

  • intraoperative cholangiography
  • intraoperative ultrasound
  • intraoperative cholangioscopy.

1. Cholangiography (fluoroscopy)

It is considered the procedure of choice for the intraoperative radiological assessment of EHBD. It has a 98-100% specificity and sensitivity for the detection of CBD stones. The iodinated contrast substance is injected either through the gallbladder (cholecysto-cholangiography) or, more frequently, through the cystic duct. Thus, highly accurate real-time images of both the stones and bile duct anatomy are obtained.

2. Intraoperative ultrasound – possible as part of the open approach, as well as during laparoscopy (through special transducers 10-12 mm in diameter). It has a sensitivity and specificity of 85-100% and can be performed in 5-10 minutes, also providing real-time images.

3. Choledochoscopy allows the visual exploration of the bile ducts through a transcystic approach or through the choledochotomy site. For the first approach variant, the cystic duct caliber should be large enough to allow the passage of the choledoscope (3-5 mm) (there is also the possibility of previous pneumatic balloon dilation of the cystic duct). Images are transmitted either to a separate monitor or to the laparoscopy monitor, with a video mixer. The disadvantage of the transcystic approach is difficult (sometimes impossible) access upstream of the cystic duct-common hepatic duct junction (a long cystic duct, at a sharp angle with the CBD).

TREATMENT

Common bile duct stones are most frequently detected during the investigations preceding cholecystectomy, but they can also be detected intraoperatively or (worse), postoperatively.

-Preoperatively detected CBD stones:

There are three therapeutic options for their removal:

a. ERCP + sphincterotomy, endoscopic extraction

b. Laparoscopic approach (transcystic or choledochotomy)

c. Open surgical approach (transcystic or choledochotomy).

a. Endoscopic treatment

With the introduction of endoscopic sphincterotomy (ES) in 1974, surgical indications for CBDS were significantly reduced, so that ERCP, with or without endoscopic sphincterotomy (ES), is currently considered the standard technique for the removal of common bile duct stones.

After deep canulation of the CBD under endoscopic control, electrosection (high frequency current) of the papillary sphincter fibers along an average length of 15 mm is performed with a sphincterotome. Thus, a wide access to the common bile duct lumen is obtained, which is required for the extraction of the stones. These can be captured using special basket or balloon catheters (Dormia and Foley, respectively). These are inserted under radiological control upstream of the stones that are extracted (after closure of the basket or inflation of the balloon) through the ES orifice.

Finally, 90-95% of calculi can be successfully extracted.

For “difficult” stones (larger than 15 mm), the following endoscopic solutions are available:

  • mechanical lithotripsy
  • electrohydraulic lithotripsy
  • laser lithotripsy
  • extracorporeal lithotripsy.

All these methods are used for large stones (> 15 mm, exceeding the sphincterotomy length) or in the presence of biliary strictures that do not allow evacuation. They can generate complications in 8-10% of the cases (cholangitis, acute pancreatitis, hemorrhage or even duct lesions). Electrohydraulic and laser lithotripsy are procedures performed under direct visual cholangioscopic control. The fragmentation and complete removal of large stones require repeated sessions. These procedures are available only in tertiary centers.

Endoscopic treatment variants:

  • - The pneumatic dilation of the papillary sphincter:

It uses balloons that are inflated in the papilla up to 8-12 mm diameters, in order to gain access to the CBD, after which the stones are extracted. The technique is not intended for routine use (less effective and with an increased risk of post-procedure pancreatitis). It can be applied as an alternative to ES in patients with contraindications (untreatable coagulopathies) or as a complement to limited ES, when for anatomical reasons this cannot reach the usual length (juxtapapillary duodenal diverticulum).

  • - Temporary endoscopic biliary drainage:

For patients with multiple stones (or multiple fragments resulting from lithotripsy), which require several sessions to ensure CBD vacuity, the placement of a plastic endoprosthesis or a nasobiliary drain can ensure temporary inter-procedure biliary drainage (internal or external).

In the case of very fragile patients (advanced age, important comorbidities), at high risk for both surgery and laborious endoscopic procedures, there is also the option of placing an endoprosthesis with or without treatment with bile acids (e.g., ursodeoxycholic acid), for litholysis. In case of an improved general state after 60-90 days, the endoscopic extraction of stones (which depending on composition may have been dissolved/fragmented following the mentioned treatment) can be reattempted. If this is not the case, the endoprosthesis can be maintained permanently (being periodically replaced in case of clogging).

Despite all undeniable advantages and benefits as a first-line therapeutic modality in CBDS, endoscopic sphincterotomy may also generate early and late complications.

Early complications:

1. Acute pancreatitis

  • it occurs with a frequency of 3-5.4% of cases, particularly in young women
  • dyskinetic sphincter of Oddi
  • after the use of the precut scalpel
  • non-dilated bile ducts
  • difficult canulation
  • previous post-ERCP pancreatitis episodes.

2. Hemorrhage

Occurring after 2-5% of ESs, it is considered a post-procedure complication only when it causes melena and a 2 g decrease in hemoglobin values. A prolongation of the duration of hospitalization by more than 5 days defines moderately severe hemorrhage, and the need for surgical hemostasis and/or a prolongation of the hospital stay by 10 days indicates severe hemorrhage. Mortality is less than 1%.

The main risk factors for post-ES hemorrhagic accident can be divided into two categories:

a. patient related factors:

o coagulation disorders

o frequent in cirrhotic patients

o cardiac patients receiving chronic anticoagulant treatment

o patients with chronic renal failure.

For the last category of patients, it is recommended to stop treatment 7-10 days before ES. Anatomical particularities may also increase the risk of hemorrhage, i.e., a juxta- or even intradiverticular papilla.

b. technique related factors:

o re-sphincterotomy (enlargement of a previous ES)

o incorrect orientation (in the case of inexperienced

endoscopists) of the sphincter section (correct between 11

and 1 o’clock), in relation to the longitudinal axis of the

terminal common bile duct. 3. Cholangitis (frequency of 1-2% of cases) occurs when post-procedure biliary drainage is insufficient (stones or residual fragments, post-ES papillary edema). 4. Perforation (0.3-1%) can be favored by the anatomical particularities of the case (juxtapapillary diverticulum), technique (re-sphincterotomy) or the operator’s technical skills (too long ES, incorrect orientation – beyond 10 o’clock). 5. Impaction of the catheter.Dormia impaction at the level of the papillary orifice may occur when attempting to extract a stone exceeding the diameter of the sectioned papilla, which has not been fragmented intraductally. It may require surgery (duodenotomy, enlargement of ES, followed by sphincteroplasty).

Late complications:

Papillary stenosis occurs after too short ESs, which in time evolve with fibrous scarring, towards stenosis. The therapeutic solution is a sufficiently large re-sphincterotomy.

Since complications generated by ERCP/ES, although rare, are not exceptional (10% morbidity, less than 0.5% mortality), strict observance of indications and contraindications (keeping diagnostic ERCP to the necessary minimum – previous endoscopic ultrasound or MRC for the confirmation of CBDS), as well as the endoscopist’s experience and skills make ERCP/ES the reference procedure in the treatment of CBD stones.

Nevertheless, in 5-15% of cases with mixed gallbladder and common bile duct stones, the choledochal component is managed surgically.

Surgical treatment:

a. The laparoscopic approach of common bile duct stones:

exploration and clearance

Although its use is limited to centers with great experience in advanced laparoscopic surgery, the concomitant laparoscopic treatment of cholecystolithiasis and choledocholithiasis (“all in one” laparoscopic approach or “single stage procedure”) seems to be the ideal solution. The shortest duration of hospitalization, the lowest morbidity, a higher comfort for the patient and optimal cost effectiveness were the results of cholecystectomy with exploration/clearance of CBD stones through the cystic duct (or through “ideal choledochotomy”), both of which by laparoscopic approach.

1. Transcystic CBD exploration/clearance by laparoscopic approach:

Indications Failure of endoscopic CBD stone extraction

Contraindications of choledochotomy:

  • A CBD diameter < 6mm
  • Sclerosing pediculitis
  • Impossibility to suture the choledochotomy site Stones less than 6-8 mm in diameter

Contraindications  Stones > 6 mm in diameter

  • Intrahepatic lithiasis
  • A cystic duct caliber < 4 mm
  • A cystic duct with posterior insertion
  • A cystic duct with distal insertion (double-barrel shotgun)

Transcystic approach is the first option, because it is less invasive, more rapid, cheaper, with a lower morbidity and shorter postoperative evolution, easier for the patient.

Technique:

The exploratory stage (cholangiography) is followed by the therapeutic stage; both can be performed either percutaneously or through a 5 mm trocar. After transcystic access to the CBD has been established, through the inserted catheter the removal of small stones (less than 4 mm in diameter) is initially attempted by lavage with saline, under moderate pressure; previous administration of 1 mg glucagon i.v., with consecutive relaxation of the oddian sphincter, may push small stones transpapillary. CBD vacuity is checked by control cholangiography or/and choledochoscopy. In case of failure or of larger stones (7-8 mm in diameter), extraction with Dormia orFoley catheters (after pneumatic balloon dilation, up to maximum 8 mm, of the cystic duct), is usually successful. For larger stones, intraductal fragmentation procedures are available (electrohydraulic lithotripsy is preferred). CBD vacuity is re-checked by cholangiography or/and choledochoscopy. The disadvantage and limitations of cholangioscopy result from limited access (depending on the anatomic variant of cystic duct-common hepatic duct junction) to the common hepatic duct and upstream of it; in addition, intraoperative cholangiography provides valuable information on the anatomy of the biliary tree. The confirmation of complete CBD vacuity allows for clipping and sectioning of the cystic duct and cholecystectomy. Leaving a transcystic-duct drainage catheter in place for 15-18 days is also possible. In case of failed transcystic approach, choledochotomy is required.

2. Laparoscopic choledochotomy:

A particularly effective procedure in the exploration and removal of CBDS, which requires advanced technical skills. Indications  A large number of stones

  • Stones situated proximally to the cystic duct insertion
  • Stones larger than 8 mm in diameter
  • Impossibility of transcystic access
  • Failure of transcystic approach
  • Contraindications of transcystic approach

Contraindications  A CBD caliber < 5-6 mm

  • Pediculitis/peripediculitis that makes impossible the dissection and identification of CBD
  • Impossibility of CBD suture
  • Portal hypertension (“pericholedochal varices”)

Technique: After the CBD is visualized,

  • two guiding threads are placed (optional) – traction on the anterior side

of the supraduodenal common bile duct.

  • longitudinal supraduodenal choledochotomy along the long axis of the

duct is performed, whose length will not exceed the maximum diameter of the common bile duct or of the stone to be removed. From this point onwards, the extraction procedures are similar to those already described.

  • first, common bile duct lavage under pressure is carried out, in order to

drive small stones through the papilla or through the choledochotomy site. However, there is a risk for these to be mobilized upstream, intrahepatically.

  • then follows the instrumental extraction of the stones (basket or balloon

catheters– Dormia, Foley, Fogarty) under choledochoscopic control.

  • large stones require previous intraductal fragmentation (lithotripsy).
  • finally, checking complete CBD vacuity by choledochoscopy and

cholangiography is compulsory.

Once this objective attained, there are two modalities to close the

choledochotomy:

I.Choledochotomy with primary coledochorrhaphy – primary suture, without biliary drainage, of the choledochotomy site. Primary choledochorrhaphy, which was avoided in the past, is currently increasingly used; it is essential that, using all available imaging means (highly accurate cholangiography, cholangioscopy), CBD vacuity and especially, a permeable papilla with normal caliber and functionality, should be confirmed. Meeting these conditions, primary choledochorrhaphy proved to be superior to other procedures (shorter duration of hospitalization, increased comfort for the patient, low morbidity, cost-efficiency). This procedure requires experience in advanced laparoscopic surgery; it consists of a tight suture, preferably with interrupted stitches (possibly with running suture as well), and intracorporeal knots (fine absorbable suture – polyglycolic acid or PDS, 4–0 or 5-0).

II. External drainage of the common bile duct with T- tube is the second option, which has certain advantages compared to the first one: effective biliary decompression in case of papillary edema or residual stone fragments; it allows postoperative radiological control (T-tube cholangiography); it provides easy access for the extraction of potential residual stones without using postoperative endoscopic sphincterotomy.

Technique:

Usually, 14 Fr T-tubes are used; after carefully inserting the short branch of the tube in the CBD, the choledochotomy is sutured tightly around the tube, with fine absorbable threads (4.0/5.0 PDS). The long end of the tube will be externalized through the percutaneous orifice of one of the 5 mm trocars, which allows the most direct and declivous trajectory. The procedure ends with control T-tube cholangiography. Thus, an effective external drainage of the common bile duct has been obtained. This will be removed at 10-14 days postoperatively, after a final control cholangiography, which will confirm the vacuity of the biliary tree.

b.The open (classic) surgical approach for common bile duct stones:

Indications for open choledochotomy:

1. Failure or contraindications of preoperative ERCP

2. Failure or contraindications of laparoscopic approach

3. Impossible access to endoscopy or/and laparoscopy

4. Detection of CBDS during open cholecystectomy

5. Large stones

6. Impacted stones in the papilla

7. Indications for biliodigestive derivation:

  • CBD rock paving
  • marked CBD dilations (≥ 20 mm)
  • benign CBD stenosis (chronic pancreatitis)
  • primary (autochthonous) CBD stones 8. Gastric resection with Billroth II reconstruction or total gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction 9. Gastroenteroanastomosis 10. Juxtapapillary duodenal diverticulum.

Technically and tactically, the successive steps of CBD exploration, clearance (choledochotomy and intraoperative cholangiography, instrumental extraction), and choledochotomy closure (primary suture or T-tube external biliary drainage) are similar to those already described for laparoscopic approach. It should not be forgotten that laparoscopy has borrowed the technical maneuvers and therapeutic principles from the classical procedures, not the other way around. The contraindications of open CBD exploration are as important as its indications. Contraindications 1. Portal hypertension – from cirrhosis or portal vein of choledochotomy thrombosis – here the major risk is the development (also valid for of an exuberant collateral venous circulation in the laparoscopic hepatic pedicle (“pericholedochal varices”), which, approach) due to extreme hemorrhagic risk, jeopardizes any

attempt of dissection at this level;

2. A CBD caliber smaller than 5-6 mm – high risk

of late stenosis at the common bile duct suture site;

3. Sclerosing pediculitis – sclero-inflammatory

changes make impossible the dissection and

identification of the CBD;

4. Acute cholangitis with septic shock – emergency

biliary decompression, initially minimally invasive

(endoscopic) and subsequently surgical, is required.

In rare cases, when none of the procedures previously described for choledochotomy (instrumental stone extraction, lithotripsy, etc.) has resulted in the mobilization of the impacted stone in the papilla, the only technical solution is transduodenal sphincterotomy (with stone extraction and sphincteroplasty). For this, after the exact localization by palpation (or laparoscopic ultrasound) of the papilla and the impacted stone, duodenotomy, preferably transverse, is performed at this level (on the anterior side of D2), with the identification of the papilla, wide sphincterotomy and extraction of the impacted stone. The sphincterotomy incision will be “matured” by several fine sutures applied circularly, between the choledochal and duodenal mucosa; fine absorbable threads are used (vicryl 4-0, 5-0). Thus, Oddi sphincteroplasty is obtained, which is in fact equivalent to a large distal choledochoduodenal anastomosis. The double-layer closure of the duodenotomy will end the procedure.

INTRODUCTION – DEFINITION

Biliodigestive fistulas are aberrant connections formed between an element of the extrahepatic bile ducts (gallbladder or common bile duct) and the digestive tract (stomach, duodenum, colon).

I.INCIDENCE

Rare but not exceptional events, biliodigestive fistulas have an incidence between 1.2-5% (studies performed on large cholecystectomy series).

Of these, the vast majority arecholecystoduodenal fistulas (75 -80%).

Other types of fistulas:

  • cholecystocolic (10-12%)
  • cholecystogastric (4.2-4.9%)
  • choledochoduodenal (3.5-4.5%)
  • multiple (combined) fistulas.

II.ETIOPATHOGENY

The overwhelming majority of cholecysto-digestive fistulas are of lithiasic origin (80-90%).

Other possible pathogenic mechanisms:

o Post-traumatic biliodigestive fistulas

  • Crohn disease o Iatrogenic – cholecystostomy o Oddi sphincterotomy o Alveolar echinococcosis o Chronic duodenal ulcer o Neoplastic: - distal common bile duct cancer o Carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater o Neoplasm of the head of the pancreas o Duodenal neoplasms o Gallbladder cancer o Colon cancer.

In 80% of choledochoduodenal fistula cases in Western countries, the most common cause is the chronic duodenal ulcer (particularly posterior duodenal bulb ulcer), while in Asia biliary etiopathogeny is predominant.

a. For fistulas of lithiasic etiology, the pathogenic sequence starts with the impaction of a large stoneof the obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone (in general a macrostone). In time, recurrent episodes of acute (or subacute) cholecystitis and chronic cholecystitis with subsequent pericholecystitis (inflammatory lesions and wall alterations are the most severe at macrocholedochal level) generate inflammatory adhesions to the adjacent organs (duodenum, colon, etc.). Inside the resulting “adhesion block”, through a “decubitus lesion” the stone will penetrate the gallbladder wall and subsequently, the “digestive partner’s” adhesion-fixed wall, thus forming the biliodigestive fistula through which it will subsequently migrate.

b. For fistulas of malignant etiology, the element connecting the biliodigestive partners is tumor invasion and erosion.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

Due to their slowly progressive formation, bilio-digestive fistulas are frequently asymptomatic or paucisymptomatic. This is why they are detected on the occasion of preoperative imaging (in case of manifest cholelithiasis) or frequently, only during surgery.

Common clinical manifestations:

  • abdominal pain (epigastric, right upper quadrant), most frequently nonspecific; sometimes intermittent cramps – Konig syndrome – (migrated, obstructive large stones)
  • nausea, vomiting
  • weight loss
  • diarrhea (typical in cholecysto-colic fistulas).

Acute clinical manifestations:

  • cholangitis (pain, fever, jaundice) – as a result of contaminating septic bilio-digestive reflux (intra-biliary ascending regurgitation of colonic content – in cholecysto-colic fistulas).
  • upper digestive hemorrhage – intermittent, in small amounts (melena), usually occurring at the time of fistular mechanical erosion into the visceral wall.
  • biliary ileus:
  • a rare variant of acute bowel obstruction (1-3%) with sudden onset, abundant vomiting (initially clear bilious, later turbid bile, and finally – 12-24 hours later – fecaloid), important central abdominal distension, cessation of bowel movements, altered general state.
  • caused by migration of a large gallbladder stone (3-4 cm in diameter) through a large cholecysto-duodenal fistula, with subsequent sudden obstructive impaction at the level of the terminal ileon (60%), (exceptionally at the level of the ileo-cecal valve).

It predominantly occurs in elderly female patients (65-85 years),

with a long history of gallbladder calculi (20-40 years). Given

the precarious background on which this complication occurs,

mortality can reach values as high as 7.5-20%!

  • less common locations for the obstructive impaction of the migrated stone are the jejunum (26%), the left colon (2-8%), the upper rectum (1-2%).
  • Bouveret syndrome – occurs more rarely than the above-described biliary ileus (3.7%) and consists of the proximal obstructive impaction of a very large stone, at the level of the duodenal bulb or in the inferior duodenal flexure, after migration through a cholecysto-duodenal fistula (usually stones larger than 3 cm in diameter). Clinical manifestations are the ones typical for proximal acute bowel obstructions, with frequent vomiting, alimentary and gastric acid vomitus – in cases in which the stone obliterates the duodenal bulb, proximal to the ampulla of Vater; -in cases in which the stone impaction occurs more distally, i.e.,at the level of the second part of the duodenum or at the inferior duodenal flexure, (impaction below the ampulla of Vater), the vomitus becomes biliary and the dehydration progresses fast, with marked water-electrolyte imbalance and rapid alteration of the general state (not to mention the advanced age and the already poor physical status of these category of patients).

1. Plain abdominal X-ray, still important in gallstone ‘ileus’, where

characteristic are:

  • RIGLER’s triad (1941): o Air-fluid levels (small bowel type) o Aerobilia (air bubbles into the biliary tree) o A large radiopaque mass with atypical location (large biliary migrated calculus impacted in the terminal segment of the ileon).

TREATMENT

This is required in the case of clinically manifest biliodio-gestive, complicated fistulas and selectively, in the intra-operatively detected cases.

1. For cholecysto-duodenal or cholecysto-colic fistulas, the following

are performed:

  • cholecystectomy
  • suture of the fistular orifice (duodenal or colonic).

Technical progress has allowed the treatment of these cases by laparoscopic approach (after adequate dissection, the cholecysto-enteric fistula can be closed with a stapler for laparoscopic use).

2. For neoplastic cholecystocolic fistulas:

  • In cases in which the primary tumor is colic (right flexure or right third of transverse colon cancer), with subsequent invasion of the gallbladder, usually a right hemicolectomy with “en block”cholecystectomy should be performed when possible.
  • However, when the starting point is a gallbladder cancer, surgical resection israrely possible.

3. For choledochoduodenal fistulas generated by duodenal ulcers

(80%), there are no standard solutions:

  • Angiocholitis cases without CBD stenosis can be resolved by adequately treating ulcer with proper medication.
  • Biliary stenoses and/or cases with cholangitis, require more complex surgical procedures (2/3 gastric resection, gastro-jejunostomy, vagotomy and bilio-digestive diversions). 4. Choledochoduodenal fistulas of malignant etiology can be resolved by endoscopic stent placement (non-resectable cases) or by pancreatico-duodenectomy (in cases with resectable periampullary tumors).

Anatomy and physiology of the biliary tract

Biliary ducts are a set of canaliculi, canals and ducts through which the bile produced in the liver is transported to the duodenum.

Bile ducts are divided into:

  • intrahepatic biliary ducts
  • extrahepatic biliary ducts.

Bile secreted by the hepatocytes is transported through bile canaliculi into the bile ducts in the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct). The bile ducts, after successive junctions, form the right and left hepatic ducts. They meet to form the common hepatic duct, which unites with the cystic duct to form the main bile duct. In its distal section, the main bile duct and the pancreatic duct join to form the hepato-pancreatic duct. It opens into the duodenum through the ampulla of Vater. The accessory bile ducts include the gallbladder and the cystic duct.

Gallbladder

It’s a hollow organ, about 7-10 cm in length, located on the visceral aspect of the liver. Divided into four anatomical areas: fundus, body, infundibulum and neck.

Anatomical relations:

  • anteriorly – the anterior abdominal wall and the inferior aspect of the liver;
  • posteriorly – the transverse colon and the first two portions of the duodenum.

Arterial vascularization: provided by the cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery (>90% of cases). The cystic artery divides into two branches, anterior and posterior, at the level of the gallbladder neck. It is can always be found in Calot’s triangle, an area bound by the cystic duct, the common bile duct and the liver edge. The venous vascularization is usually represented by small veins that enter directly into the liver and less often by a cystic vein opening into the portal vein.

Lymphatic drainage: directly into the liver or into the celiac lymph nodes through Mascagni’s lymph node, located closely to the cystic artery.

Gallbladder innervation: sympathetic fibers originating from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic fibers of vagal origin and sensitive innervation through phrenic nerve fibers. The gallbladder innervation is in close contact with the cystic artery.

Biliary ducts

The biliary ducts transport the bile from the liver to the intestine. They are divided into intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.

The intrahepatic bile ducts result from bile canaliculi opening into the bile ducts in the portal triads. By successive junctions, the intrahepatic bile ducts form the right and left hepatic ducts.

The extrahepatic bile ducts include the right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, cystic duct and main bile duct. The terminal segment of the main bile duct joins the pancreatic duct and enters the 2nd portion of the duodenum through the sphincter of Oddi.

The right and left hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct. It measures between 1 and 4 cm in length and is located at the right of the hepatic artery and anteriorly of the portal vein. It joins with the cystic duct to form the main bile duct.

The cystic duct connects the gallbladder and common hepatic duct. It is variable in length. Its junction with the common hepatic duct has many anatomical variants.

The main bile duct is created through the junction of the common hepatic duct with the cystic duct. It varies in length between 5 and 11 cm and in diameter between 4 and 10 mm. It can be divided into three portions: supraduodenal, retroduodenal and intrapancreatic. The intrapancreatic portion joins the pancreatic duct to form a common duct. There are three possible configurations of this junction: more frequently, in approximately 70% of the cases, the two ducts meet outside the duodenal wall, while in 20% of cases the junction takes place in the duodenal wall and in about 10% of the cases they do not join at all and open into the duodenum through two separate orifices.

The arterial vascularisation of the extrahepatic biliary tract is provided distally by the gastroduodenal artery and the posterior pancreaticoduodenal artery and proximally by the hepatic artery.

The venous drainage is achieved through the paracholedochal venous plexus opening into the portal vein.

The autonomic innervation of the extrahepatic bile ducts includes parasympathetic vagal fibers and sympathetic fibers originating in the celiac plexus.

Biliary tract physiology

The liver produces about 500-1000 ml of bile daily. Bile contains water, electrolytes, bile salts, bile pigments, proteins and lipids. Approximately 80% of the total amount of bile secreted is reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, while the rest, up to 95%, is absorbed in the colon.

  • The extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts: responsible for the

transportation of bile from the liver into the small intestine

-The gallbladder: plays a role in storing and concentrating the bile. The gallbladder contractions are stimulated by the vagal parasympathetic innervation and cholecystokinin and inhibited by the sympathetic innervation, somatostatin and VIP (vasoactive intestinal polypeptide).

-The sphincter of Oddi: regulates the release of bile into the duodenum and prevents the reflux of bile in the biliary ducts.

The neoplastic diseases of the biliary structures are divided into two categories: bile duct neoplasm or cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder neoplasm.

Cholangiocarcinoma

Nadim Al Hajjar

Epidemiology

Cholangiocarcinoma accounts for less than 2% of all primary tumors. It accounts for 10-15% of all primary liver tumors, being the second most frequent primary tumor after the hepatocarcinoma. The incidence and mortality rates of cholangiocarcinoma have increased in the past 40 years. Most of these patients are between the ages of 40 and 65 years with an average of 50 years. The sex ratio in this condition is 54% males; the mortality rate is higher in women.

Etiology

A clear etiology is difficult to determine in most cases. Chronic inflammation of the biliary tract appears to be linked to the development of cancer. Genetic mutations occurring throughout life are more frequently associated with cancer occurrence than inherited mutations. Mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene have been linked with the development of cancer of the biliary tract.

Risk Factors

Several risk factors are involved in the development of cancer of the biliary tract. Most of these factors have in common the chronic inflammation of the biliary tract.

* chronic liver and bile duct diseases: primary sclerosing cholangitis,

ductal stones, choledochal cysts, anatomic variants of the main bile

duct and pancreatic duct, cirrhosis

* inflammatory bowel disease

* old age

* obesity

* alcohol consumption and smoking

* exposure to carcinogenic chemicals.

Classification of cholangiocarcinoma

It is classified into three categories according to location:

* intrahepatic

* perihilar

* distal. Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. This type develops from branches of the intrahepatic biliary tree. It is similar to the neoplasm originating in the hepatocyte (hepatocarcinoma) and is usually treated similarly. It accounts for about 10% of all cholangiocarcinoma cases. Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. Known as Klatskin tumor. It develops from the bile ducts located in the hepatic hilum. This is the most common form, accounting for about 60-70% of all bile duct tumours.

The Bismuth classification ofperihilar cholangiocarcinoma includes 5 categories, depending on tumor location:

  • Bismuth I– limited to the common hepatic duct, below the level of the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts;
  • Bismuth II– involves the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts;
  • Bismuth IIIa – involves the confluence and the right hepatic duct;
  • Bismuth IIIb– involves the confluence and the left hepatic duct;
  • Bismuth IV– involves both right and left hepatic ducts ORmultifocal involvement.

The symptoms are similar to those of pancreatic head tumors. It represents about 20-30% of the all cholangiocarcinomas. Belongs to the group of extrahepatic cholagiocarcinomas together with the perihilar form.

Histology and macroscopy

Approximately 95% of biliary tumors are malignant. Of these, most are adenocarcinomas. Adenocarcinomas originate in the mucous gland cells lining the walls of the bile ducts. Less frequently, other types of carcinomas can also be found: sarcomas, lymphomas, small cell neoplasms, adenosquamous and squamous carcinoma. Among the benign tumors, the most common are hamartomas and adenomas.

From a macroscopic viewpoint, localized tumors have a nodular growth type with periductal infiltration and share the same macroscopic aspect with hepatocarcinomas.Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas usually infiltrate the bile duct walls and in time lead to lumen stenosis.

Diagnosis

Clinical diagnosis

Colangiocarcinomas are mostly asymptomatic in the early stages of development. Symptoms occur when the tumors increases in size or has an extrahepatic location, leading to obstruction of bile duct lumen.

Symptoms and signs that occur most frequently are:

  • upper abdominal pain
  • jaundice
  • choluria
  • acholic stools
  • weight loss, nausea and vomiting
  • asthenia, fatigue.

The onset of jaundice requires making the differential diagnosis between a benign and a malignant obstructive jaundice. These two types of jaundice are different in terms of clinical features and paraclinical results:

  • the benign etiology: it is characterized by sudden onset of symptoms, with fever and biliary colic. Physical examination: positive Murphy sign with right upper quadrant pain on palpation, aggravated by forced inspiration. Lab tests: positive inflammatory markers. Imaging findings: gallbladder or bile duct lithiasis.
  • the malignant etiology: insidious onset, without pain or fever, slow progression. Positive Curvoisier-Terrier sign, signifying an enlarged, palpable and painless gallbladder. Paraclinical findings: positive tumor markers; tumoral masses, lymphadenopathy, ascites as imaging findings.

The symptoms of bile duct cancer vary depending on the tumor site within the biliary tree.

  • the intrahepatic localization exhibits nonspecific symptoms: upper abdominal pain, asthenia, fatigue, cachexia.
  • theperihilar cholangiocarcinoma is usually associated with biliary obstruction with painless jaundice (approximately 90%) and cholestasis: jaundice, pruritus, acholic stools, choluria. Approximately 10% of patients have cholangitis and 50% have systemic symptoms: abdominal discomfort, malaise, nausea, weight loss.
  • the distal cholangiocarcinoma exhibits symptoms similar to those of the perihilar type and may mimic the symptoms of pancreatic head neoplasms. An obstruction of the common hepatobiliary duct can cause acute pancreatitis.

Laboratory investigations

The most frequent findings are cholestasis and jaundice. The usual altered tests include:

  • Bilirubin – elevated due to increased conjugated bilirubin (obstructive jaundice);
  • Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT – increased, suggesting obstruction;
  • Prothrombin time – prolonged (the biliary obstruction affects coagulation);
  • Transaminases – normal or slightly elevated;
  • INR - normal or elevated;

 The tumor markers that may be found elevated are CA 19-9,

CA-125, CEA and AFP. Although usually these markers indicate

the presence of tumors, they are not specific for cholangiocarcinoma

and may be elevated in other cancers or other disorders. On the other

hand, low levels of these markers do not exclude completely the

cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis.

Imaging diagnosis

The imaging examinations are useful in the identification and localization of an obstruction of the biliary tree. Nevertheless, some examinations cannot discriminate between benign and malignant etiologies. Another important role of imaging techniques is preoperatory staging. The most efficient and most commonly used techniques in diagnosing and staging bile duct neoplasms are:

1.Ultrasonography

Abdominal ultrasonography is usually the first imaging examination for biliary obstruction or suspected liver disease. The intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma may be identified as a tumoral mass. In contrast, hilar and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas are often infiltrative lesions that are difficult to detect. On ultrasonography, the non-union of the dilated right and left hepatic ducts may be seen without an identifiable mass. The reported sensitivity of ultrasonography in detecting ductal masses or mural thickening in hilar and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas is up to 87%–96% in some series, but depends on the skill of the investigator.

2. Computed tomography

Computed tomography (CT) can show bile duct dilation and a tumoral mass, bile duct wall thickening, or intraductal tissue in exophytic, infiltrative and polypoid cholangiocarcinomas, respectively.

3. Magnetic resonance imaging, MRI with MRCP

MRI with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is usually considered the modality of choice in the diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma because of its high contrast resolution, multiplanar capability, and its ability to determine the parenchymal, biliary, and vascular extension. Several studies, including a meta-analysis, have shown that MRI has a sensitivity and a specificity >90% in diagnosing biliary obstruction.

On gadolinium-enhanced MRI, the lesions are hypovascular and show progressive and concentric filling with contrast material. Associated findings include hepatic capsular retraction, vascular encasement that may lead to lobar atrophy, and dilatation of peripheral bile ducts. An intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma may be difficult to differentiate from a metastasis (especially a metastasis from a foregut adenocarcinoma) on imaging and on histology.

4. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)

It has been reported that endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) improves the diagnosis between malignant and benign strictures relative to MRCP and CT. Endoscopic ultrasound can be used for fine-needle aspiration of strictures with variable reported sensitivities of 25%-91% and specificities of 89%-100%.

5. Cholangiography

Because of their invasiveness, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) and percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography are replaced by MRCP, CT, and EUS in assessing the morphology of the bile ducts in patients with suspected biliary obstruction. To distinguish benign from malignant biliary strictures, however, ERCP can be used to provide tissue samples through different methods, including brush cytology, fine-needle aspiration, and transpapillary biopsy.

6. Positron emission tomography

Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET) permits the detection of cholangiocarcinomas because of the high uptake of glucose and the low activity of glucose-6-phosphatase in cholangiocarcinoma. Since many hilar and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas are infiltrative, these tumors are not readily detected by PET. The specificity of PET is limited because infectious and inflammatory lesions may show a high FDG uptake.

Staging

The staging system used for cholangiocarcinoma is the TNM system. Intrahepatic tumors are staged differently from extrahepatic ones, which in turn can be classified into two different categories: perihilar and distal. The TNM system takes into account three parameters:

  • T – describes the extension of the tumor in the duct and into adjacent tissues and organs;
  • N – describes the extension to locoregional lymph nodes;
  • M – encodes the presence of metastases in other organs.

Treatment

Bile duct tumors can be treated using 4 main therapeutic categories:

a) Surgery

b) Chemotherapy

c) Radiotherapy

d) Palliation.

a. Surgery

Surgical procedures for cholangiocarcinomas can be either curative or palliative. Potentially curative surgery is reserved for neoplasms classified as “resectable” after investigations, meaning that complete resection is possible. Only a small proportion of biliary neoplasms are resectable at diagnosis. Tumors that have exceeded the resectable level can be treated with palliative surgery, which aims for the surgical control of symptoms.

Because of different possible localizations of cholangiocarcinomas within the biliary tree, the surgical treatment will vary accordingly.

-Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma:

Surgical resection remains the only curative treatment for patients with resectable tumors of this localization. Most patients are inoperable because their tumor is too advanced at the time of diagnosis. Surgery is contraindicated in case of multiple tumors, periportal adenopathy and distant metastases.

The resection margin that may ensure maximum survival and a minimal relapse rate is not clearly established. Most recent studies report that R0 resection margins are associated with significantly higher survival rates and lower local recurrence rate when compared to R1 or R2 resection margins. Ensuring R0 resection margins in patients without distant metastases (N0) was associated with a higher survival rate whereas the R0 margin in patients with distant metastases did not significantly influence survival (median survival 18 vs. 13 months).

In patients with resectable biliary cancer, radical surgery implies segmental hepatic resection or hepatectomy. Extended liver resection with resection of the biliary confluence and the caudate lobe is recommended for tumors involving the two hepatic ducts.

The preoperative assessment should take into account the multifocal intrahepatic tumors, lymph node and distant metastases. These are considered contraindications for surgery. However, surgical treatment can be considered even in these patients in carefully selected cases.

-Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma:

Surgical resection with R0 resection margins remains the only treatment modality with curative intent in patients with resectable tumors. This type of cholangiocarcinoma has a 20 to 42% 5-year survival after surgery. The resection margin and lymph node involvement are survival predictive factors.

In the case of perihilar tumors, the recommended approach is resection of the affected biliary tract in association with liver resection. Frequently, parts of the liver, the gall bladder and sometimes local lymph nodes and parts of the intestine and pancreas are resected alongside the affected biliary tree. Restoration of bile flow is achieved by anastomosis of the biliary stump to an intestinal loop.

-Distal cholangiocarcinoma:

In case of distally located neoplasms, an important issue concerns the involvement of the pancreas and duodenum. A surgical intervention performed for a tumor localized distally on the common bile duct also involves resection of the duodenum and of the pancreatic head. This type of intervention was first described by Whipple; it implies block resection of the main bile duct, gallbladder, duodenum, antrum of the stomach and head of the pancreas and anastomosis of the cephalic portion of the pancreas to the stomach or jejunum, gastro-jejunal and hepatico-jejunal anastomosis. The Traverso-Longmire procedure is a variant of this intervention with preservation of the pylorus as opposed to the Whipple intervention.

The biliary cancer surgery involves major surgery with multiorgan involvement, leading to an increased complication rate. The most common postoperative complications in cholangiocarcinoma surgery are the immediate complications due to postoperative bleeding, anastomotic fistulas and liver injury with elevated liver enzymes. The long-term complications usually include anastomotic stenoses.

b, c. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy

The role of chemotherapy and radiotherapy in the treatment of cholangiocarcinoma is not well defined. Recent studies have shown a benefit in survival time in patients receiving chemotherapy associated with surgery and radiotherapy. The benefit of chemotherapy and radiotherapy becomes more apparent with more advanced tumor stages and with higher risk of locoregional recurrence.

d. Palliative treatment

In case of tumors beyond surgery, measures should be taken to establish continuity of the biliary tree and to maintain bile flow. For the intrahepatic type, in case of partial blockage of the biliary tree, a percutaneous external hepatic drainage can be placed under ultrasound guidance. For extrahepatic tumors, restoration of the bile flow is achieved by placing stents through ERCP or by performing a biliary-digestive anastomosis upstream from the tumor. The liver stents and drains should be replaced approximately every 3-4 months to avoid clogging the lumen. Unresectable intrahepatic tumors may benefit from tumor ablation procedures and chemoembolization. In patients with advanced disease, the issue of chronic pain treatment should be addressed.

Gallbladder neoplasms

Nadim Al Hajjar

The gallbladder neoplasm is the most common and most aggressive form of biliary cancer.

Epidemiology

The gallbladder neoplasm is the 5th most common cancer of the gastrointestinal tract and the most frequent biliary tract malignancy. Of all patients having undergone cholecystectomy for gallstones, around 0.5-1% of patients end up being diagnosed with gallbladder cancer. The incidence increases with age. The 5-year survival is around 5-10% for this type of malignancy. Only about 1 in 5 patients is diagnosed at an early stage of disease.

Etiology and risk factors

A clear etiology is difficult to determine in most cases. Chronic inflammation of the gall bladder appears to be related to cancer development. De novo genetic mutations are more frequently associated with cancer occurrence than hereditary mutations.

Several risk factors are involved in the development of gallbladder cancer. Many of these induce chronic inflammation of the gallbladder wall:

* Gallstones: the most important risk factor, leads to chronic

inflammation of the gallbladder wall. Approximately 3 out of 4

patients with gallbladder cancer are also found with gallstones at the

time of diagnosis.

* Porcelain-gallbladder: bladder wall calcification due to chronic

inflammation. There is a risk of cancer development of approximately

6% compared to 1% in patients without calcification.

* Bile duct abnormalities.

* Gallbladder polyps.

* Choledochal cysts.

* Inflammatory bowel disease.

* Obesity.

* The female sex.

Histology and macroscopical appearance

Most tumors are adenocarcinomas, in around 90% of cases, followed by squamous cell carcinomas (5-10%) and undifferentiated carcinomas (about 5%). Macroscopically, the gallbladder carcinoma infiltrates the gallbladder wall and, relatively quickly, also the adjacent organs, especially the liver.

Clinical diagnosis

Gallbladder cancer is usually diagnosed in an advanced stage. This type of carcinoma is aggressive and tends to spread quickly to nearby organs. The clinical symptoms mimicking a biliary colic or chronic cholecystitis is another factor leading to a late diagnosis. Therefore, approximately 50% of patients are diagnosed after cholecystectomy.

Symptoms and signs that occur most frequently are:

* abdominal pain: at diagnosis, most patients experience abdominal

pain usually located in the right upper quadrant;

* jaundice: through the mechanism of biliary obstruction; the presence

of jaundice is associated with a poor prognosis;

* nausea, vomiting;

* weight loss;

* asthenia, fatigue;

* palpable tumor.

Laboratory Investigations

  • Bilirubin – elevated due to increased conjugated bilirubin (obstructive jaundice);
  • Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT – increased, suggesting obstruction;
  • Prothrombin time – prolonged ( the biliary obstruction affects coagulation);
  • Transaminases – normal or slightly elevated;
  • INR – normal or elevated;
  • The tumor markers which may be elevated are CA 19-9 and CEA.. CA 19-9 values above 20 units / mL and CEA above 4.0 ng / mL are suggestive of this diagnosis. However, by the time these markers are found elevated in the blood, the cancer is already in an advanced stage. These markers are not specific for gallbladder cancer.

Imaging diagnosis

1.Abdominal ultrasound– most often it is the first imaging test used, because of itsavailability.

2.Computed tomography (CT) – provides accurate information on the presence or absence of obstruction and tumor extension to other nearby or distant organs.

3.Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) – advantages and disadvantages similar to those of the CT examination. It allows preoperative staging.

4.PET-CT useful in assessing local adenopathies

5.Cholangiography is recommended in patients presenting with jaundice, in order to assess hepatic and biliary tract invasion. For diagnostic purposes, magnetic resonance cholangiography is preferred before ERCP.

Staging

The TNM system is used in the staging of gallbladder cancer. It takes into account tumor invasion in the gallbladder wall and adjacent organs (T), lymph node involvement (N) and the presence of distant metastases (M).

Gallbladder cancer treatment

Surgery

Complete surgical resection with negative resection margins (R0) is the gold standard treatment of resectable gallbladder tumors. The surgical resection implies the association of cholecystectomy with liver resection limited to segments IV and V and periportal lymphadenectomy. Extended liver resection and bile duct resection may be necessary in patients with advanced disease in order to obtain negative resection margins. In these cases, the extended resection may include the duodenum or pancreas or any other organ in which the tumor has spread.

If the diagnosis is made after a cholecystectomy for an apparently benign disease, early-stage tumors (T1a) will not require a new intervention for extended resection. In case of advanced disease, a new intervention is required for extended resection.

The classical approach is preferred to laparoscopy in cases where the diagnosis was made before surgery. In case of a postoperative diagnosis, classical laparotomy is preferable for the second intervention.

Chemotherapy

Chemotherapy for gallbladder neoplasm is used pre- and postoperatively. Preoperative chemotherapy cannot by itself induce complete tumor remission; instead, it stops its development and decreases tumor size. Postoperative chemotherapy is used to minimize the risk of relapse.

Radiotherapy

Postoperative radiotherapy offers the greatest benefit to patients with at least stage T2 tumors. Studies have shown that there is no need for radiotherapy in T1, N0 patients.

Unresectable tumors

Gallbladder tumors usually exhibit distant metastasis or invasion in the celiac or aortocaval lymph nodes. For these patients, the options are limited to chemotherapy and palliative care.

In patients with unresectable tumors and biliary obstruction, biliary drainage should be performed before starting chemotherapy. Biliary drainage followed by chemotherapy leads to an improved quality of life.
